title: Quantify your Project Management Impact: The 4 Category Framework
description:
Most PMs know they're supposed to show impact with numbers. Almost none of them know where those numbers actually come from.

In this video, I break down the 4 categories of metrics that actually get recruiters and hiring managers to notice your CV and LinkedIn profile, why each one matters to a business (not just why it sounds good), and exactly how to find your own numbers even if you don't think you have any.

What I cover:
* The 4 categories every PM should be quantifying: scale, stakes, people, and outcome
* Why scale is the weakest category on its own, and what to pair it with
* How to prove impact even when you don't have a clean percentage to show for it
* The exact questions to ask yourself (and your manager) to dig up numbers you already have
* A simple way to start tracking your own impact so you're never starting from zero again
* Real examples from my own PM career across banking, energy, and mobility included throughout, so you can see what this actually looks like outside of theory.

transcript: If you are a project manager, you probably came across this advice a couple of times already. Show real impact on your CV and on LinkedIn. Prove with numbers what outcomes you've achieved instead of just describing a task. But here's the thing. No one tells you how to actually do that. Where do you even get the numbers from? Are you supposed to make them up? And which numbers do recruiters care about? In this video, I'll walk you through the four categories of metrics. Which numbers matter? And how to find them so that recruiters start to notice and trust you. Let's get into it. Project managers are honestly some of the worst at this. We manage everyone else's visible output. The engineers write the code, the designers designed interface, and then it's time to talk about our own input and own impact, and we suddenly go quiet because we have been trained to give all of the credit to our team. But in order to stay competitive in today's job market, as project managers need to put ourselves out there visibly. Now, most impact advice stops at add a number to your bullet. And that's not wrong, but it's also not very practical. Not every number carries the same weight and not every number proves the same thing about you. So I broke this down into four categories specifically designed around what project management work looks like. Scale, stakes, people, and outcome. For each category, I tell you exactly why it matters to a business, not just why it sounds impressive. And I'll give you real examples from my old career so you can see what it looks like in practice and not just in theory. Category one, scale. The first category is scale. This is your budget size, team size, how many stakeholders you manage, how many work streams or markets you touched with that project. Now, why does that matter to a business? Basically, the clearest proxy of how much risk and responsibility a business was willing to hand you. A business trusts scale to people whom they believe can actually carry it. So, when a recruiter sees a scale number like that, they're not just seeing size, they're seeing clear evidence that someone already bet on you. But here's a catch about scale metrics. Scale on its own is usually the weakest of all the four categories. Saying that you let a three million project tells a recruiter that you were present for something big, but it does not tell them whether you were actually good at it. So the fix is never let a scale number stand alone. Pair it with the coordination underneath. In my case, I didn't just manage a $3 million project for an investment app. I let it across 15 cross functional stakeholders from marketing, UX, and IT with no existing road map when I started. The second part, the zero foundation. That's what shows the skill. To find your own scale numbers, you can ask yourself how many people that I directly manage or coordinate within that project team. What was the budget or resource size I was accountable for? How many markets, teams or work streams were touched by this project? These questions can uncover the scale metrics needed to set the context of the project that you were operating in for recruiters and hiring managers to understand what it was about. Category two, stakes. Category two is stakes. As the name kind of says, this is about the stakes of the project. So, how much was actually riding on it? Again, let's go through why does this matter to a business? And honestly, that's what drives real urgency and executive attention. Nobody in the seauite loses sleep about a project being big. They lose sleep over a project being risky, costing them money or reputation. Now, here is where stakes are different from scale. Scale is what you were responsible for going in. Stakes is what was at risk in case you failed. So you can have a small scale project with really big stakes and that's a very strong signal because it shows that you were trusted with pressure and not just with size. My clearest personal example for this is when I worked in banking we had to introduce negative interest rates on the accounts of customers that was a very sensitive high stakes communication challenge because get that wrong and you got a PR crisis going on and a wave of account closures. I helped building the stakeholder communication strategy for that rollout and we landed a 90% response rate way higher than we expected. That number isn't necessarily impressive because it's big. It is impressive because of what was riding on getting it wrong. We could have lost several thousands of customers. To find your own stakes numbers within that category, you can ask yourself how many people or customers were affected or would have been affected if this project had failed. What was the actual downside, financial, reputational, or regulatory if the project didn't work out? Was there a hard deadline or a point of no return in all of this? This will uncover what was riding on you leading this particular project to a success. Quick break [music] here. If you find this helpful at all, this is exactly the kind of topic I go in deeper in my videos each week. So, hit subscribe now so you don't miss out on the next one. Now, let's get back to it. Category three, people. Category three is about people. And this one's a little different from the other ones because it's the most intangible one and honestly the hardest to put a clean number on. But it's also where most of the actual project management work lives. Here's the thing about our job. We're essentially people managers even if no one officially reports to us. Whether a project fails or succeeds often rides on whether you can align stakeholders, resolve conflict, and actually get everyone pulling in the same direction. That's not just a side skill for a project manager. That is basically the real work. Now again, why does this metric matter to a business? A project gets successfully delivered because you managed to get a room full of people who didn't trust each other to pull in the same direction. And that in the end is what turns into actual business outcomes. People skills are one of the most important parts of a project management job and being able to demonstrate them, not just claim them, is what makes a hiring manager or a recruiter trust you. So, this category is basically where you're trying to surface that invisible work. Things like, did team satisfaction go up while you were running the project. Did you get specific positive feedback from the people you worked with, not just your manager, but the actual team? Did conflict on the team go down? Did people's engagement on the project improve because of something you changed? Here's another personal example. On one project, I noticed that our team meetings weren't really working for the people involved. Some people were checked out, others were talking over others, and it was just slowing everything down. So, I introduced a personality assessment for our team, not as some kind of gimmick, but to understand how everyone in the team preferred to process information and communicate. Based on the results, we restructured how we did meetings. We had shorter check-ins for some work streams and written async updates for others. If you want an actual number for the people category, you can build it. In my case, I started asking a quick one question satisfaction rating at the end of our retrospectives each month. Just something simple like, "How did this way of working feel for you on a scale from 1 to 5." That's it. 15 seconds per person anonymous. And after a few months, you have an actual trend line that you can point to. That's how I got a number like team reported meeting satisfaction improved by 15% over 3 months instead of just guessing it. But if you don't currently have something like that running, and let's be honest, most of us won't, that's totally fine, too. What you can do instead is something else specific that you can point back to that doesn't necessarily involve a number. A message one of your colleagues sent you after a really hard project. A specific detail about what actually changed. For example, engagement in the meetings went up significantly. To find your own people evidence, you can ask yourself, did the team or stakeholder satisfaction improve on something you ran? And did you ever measure it even informally? Did you get unsolicited positive feedback? You could point back to an email, a comment in a review, a Slack message. Did you notice friction on a team and change a process because of it? And can you describe specifically what changed as a result? This category will not always produce a clear percentage. But it's also not about every single bullet on your LinkedIn profile or on your CV having an actual number attached to it. It's about quantifying where you can and showing context and evidence on the other parts. It will show a hiring manager that you don't just run a project, but that you can actually hold a team together. Category four, outcome. Category four, and I'm putting this one last on purpose, is outcome. This is everything to do with revenue, cost, risk avoided, or market position. This is the strongest of the four categories by definition. If you can tie your work to a specific outcome related metric, that's the kind of number an executive pays extra attention to. But this is also the one that you need to be a little bit careful with. And here's why. As a project manager, you are very rarely single-handedly driving revenue or a better market position. rather you enable a crossf functional team to deliver just that if you claim the result as if you personally achieved that of course that would be overclaimed and a sharp recruiter might notice it and it could hurt the way they perceive you as a team player so the fix is not to avoid outcome numbers definitely not but it's to frame them honestly not I generated this but I led the workstream that delivered this again a personal example the clearest one I have from my own career is from the banking app project that I mentioned earlier that project didn't just involve of 15 cross functional stakeholders in the $3 million budget. The outcome was that it achieved the number one app rating for online deposit accounts in Germany at that time. We translated customer research into more than 10 new app features that enabled that outcome. Now, of course, I did not build all of those features myself, but I led the project and aligned the people, the stakeholders, including backend and front-end engineers, UX designers, and so on, who built those features and ship them. That framing is honest and it's still a very strong claim. To find your own outcome numbers, you can ask what changed in revenue, cost, or risk because this work happened. Did what the team built kept being used after the project ended? If you didn't own the outcome yourself, what was the specific work stream or decision you owned? That will uncover the business result that will prove that you didn't just work, but your work had an actual impact. It moved the business forward and it signals that you can do this again for another business, for a future employer. The question that I get asked more than anything else when it comes to this topic is, "Okay, but how do I find these numbers?" Here's what I would recommend. First, go back to actual feedback. Client emails, a Slack message, 360 reviews, or a recommendation from a colleague that they left for you on LinkedIn. Those can often include very specific numbers and outcomes that you can use to prove your impact. Second, you can ask your manager or your colleagues directly. something as simple as, "Hey, do you remember roughly what percentage we improved on that roll out or what that delay would have cost us if we hadn't caught it?" You can also go back to documented risk logs, pull them out from the archive, and get the numbers straight from there. Third, and this is the one that solves the problem going forward, start your own impact tracker. I do this in a simple notes app on my phone. Every time something worth remembering happens, I just put it down in one line. For example, a risk that I caught, a number that we hit, a piece of feedback I received, and so on. something like mitigated a risk today that would have cost us $50,000 or roll out adoption hit 90% way above what we expected. It only takes 15 seconds in the moment and then 6 months later when you're updating your CV or your LinkedIn you don't need to try really hard to remember but you can just scroll through that notes app and take the evidence straight from there. So that's the four categories: scale, stakes, people, outcome. And for each one of those, don't just chase the biggest number, but choose the one that's actually true, that you can own, that you can hold up in an interview if you're being asked about it. One more thing, do not just try and load your CV or your LinkedIn profile with outcome metrics. Make sure you got a mix across all four categories because here you don't want to look one-dimensional. LinkedIn profile that shows scale, stakes, people, and outcomes side by side tells a more complete story of who you are as a project manager. It shows you can handle size, you can handle pressure, but you can also actually lead people and deliver results. That's a far more convincing picture of a project manager that you're painting there. Now, knowing which numbers to use is only half the job. The other half is knowing exactly how to phrase them so they land in a LinkedIn profile or on a CV. I made a full video on that where I break down the exact formula of how to write these bullets. I'll link it right up here if you want to watch that one next. Also, I'll link a free one-page project management resume template in description down below so you can drop the numbers that you identified in this video straight into the right format that lands with project management recruiters and hiring managers. If this was helpful, hit the like button, subscribe, and let me know in the comments how it's going with the quantification of your impact. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next one.

title: Applying for jobs in 2026? 5 resume updates you NEED to make
description:
You've sent out hundreds of applications, tailored every resume, and still all you hear back is "we've decided to move forward with a different candidate."

The job market in 2026 looks very different from a few years ago. Recruiters are flooded with applications every day, and the resume that got your friend hired in 2016 is likely working against you now.

I'm Lara, a Senior Project Lead with five years in consulting and banking. I've sat on the hiring side for my own teams and projects, reviewed hundreds of applications, and coached people through rebuilding their resumes and LinkedIn profiles. 

This video is based on what I've seen work, and what I've seen fail.

What you'll learn in this video:
* The one line at the top of your resume that most people still get wrong
* A faster way to tailor every application without rewriting your whole CV
* Why showing less experience can make you look more qualified
* The simple formula I use to turn job duties into bullet points recruiters remember
* Why your LinkedIn profile might matter more than your resume right now
* The extra step that helped me land my role in banking

Whether you're switching careers, applying for your first role, or aiming for your next step up, these updates will help you stand out more in a crowded market.

transcript: How can you make sure your resume stands out in today's overcrowded job market? You keep updating it, tailoring it, sending out hundreds of applications per week, and yet you get no replies or automated messages saying, "We've decided to move forward with a different candidate this time." The thing is, today's job market looks different than just a few years back, which means you have to take into account different aspects when writing your resume today. In this video, I'll break down five of the most important aspects to include in your CV to increase your chances of finally getting hired. Let's get into it. Before we get into the five updates, a quick intro in case you're new to this channel. I'm Mara, and I've spent the last five years managing complex projects in the consulting and banking industry. For all that time, I've sat on the other side of the table for dozens of hiring rounds for my own teams and projects. Since then, I've helped people rebuild their resumes and their positioning online to land interviews. So, this isn't theory. This is what I've personally seen work and not work when reviewing hundreds of applications and coaching others. And here's why your resume needs an update in the first place. Recruiters are dealing with mass applications. They're being flooded with resumes on the daily. So, the resume that got your friend a job in 2016 is probably going to work against you in 2026. Let's fix that. Update number one, swap the address on your resume for your LinkedIn URL. Now, let's start from the top of the resume. Right at the top of your resume in the contact info, the old way was to put your home address there. The new way is to put your LinkedIn profile link there instead. Almost no company needs your street address for this stage. What a recruiter really wants is a fast way to look you up and get a fuller picture of the person you are. Your LinkedIn does that job. So, swap it out. It's a small change, but it reduces the friction for the recruiter, who will want to background check you anyways. This way, you're allowing them to get to where they want to with fewer clicks, saving their time. Also, it sets up everything else we're about to cover. Update number two, add a key accomplishment section. Right under the contact info, the old way was to jump straight into your work experience and hoping that the right details stand out. The new way is adding a short executive summary or key accomplishment section pulling your two to three most relevant wins for that specific role that you're applying for. You can think of it as a highlight reel. It gives the recruiters your strongest proof points within seconds of scanning your resume. It shows you understand exactly what they're looking for and what's important for this role. Also, let's be honest, I'm not the biggest fan of tailoring every single resume for every single job that you apply for. It's just not efficient, it's not sustainable. Instead, tailoring your key achievement section or the executive summary, it's a quick way to tailor it. It's less effort while the recruiter even faster gets the specific information they need to know for that role. Update number three, stop listing every single job you ever had. Now we get into your actual experience section of the resume. The old way was listing every single job and internship you've had since university, even the ones that have nothing to do with the role that you're applying for, just to signal your vast experience. The new way is to prioritize your most recent and most relevant roles to the one that you're applying for only. Leave the rest out. Here's why. A recruiter isn't trying to read your full career history. They are trying to answer one question fast. Is this person's background relevant for the role I'm hiring for at the moment? If your resume is full of roles from eight years ago, you're diluting the roles that matter. Also, it's a first exercise in showing the recruiter that you can identify and prioritize what actually matters, which is a skill that is needed in many roles too. So, keep the most relevant and recent roles front and center. If someone wants your full career history, that's exactly what your LinkedIn's, which is why we swapped out your address for that link so people can actually check that out. Update number four, ditch the paragraphs. Once you've decided which roles actually make the cut and land in your resume, the next question is, how do you write about them? The old way was writing full paragraphs under each role explaining your responsibilities in detail. The new way is short, scannable bullet points on a one-column resume. Keep in mind, most of the time recruiters do not read a resume line by line, but they rather scan them. If your experience section looked like a wall of text, most people would just skip it entirely. It's not very pleasant for the eye. It kind of signals to your brain like, "Oh my god, there's a lot of dense information with no breaks in between, and I'd rather not." Instead, use bullet points. They should be short, specific, easy to scan in a second or two. Update number five, describe impact. And now that your bullet points are short, we got to make sure that what is in them earns its place. The old way was listing your responsibilities. Things like, "Responsible for managing timeline." Or, "Supported the delivery of key projects." The new way is describing the outcome of what you did, including clear numbers and specific metrics that show just that wherever you can. This is the one I see people get wrong the most, and it's the difference that actually gets you noticed. They want to know what changed because you were there. The formula I give people to write their bullet points in a specific way that lands with recruiters is the following: action plus context plus outcome. So, instead of saying, "I managed a marketing campaign." you can say something like, "Led a product launch campaign across three markets, growing sign-ups by 40% in the first quarter." So, what's the action? You leading a product launch campaign. What's the context? You were leading it across three markets. And finally, what was the outcome? What actually changed because of that? The sign-ups grew by 40% in the first quarter. It's the same experience, but it gives a completely different signal. It shows that what you do has an impact for a business. Whenever I reviewed candidates for our own team or our own projects, this was consistently the biggest difference between two candidates who had almost identical backgrounds otherwise. One of them, I could actually picture adding value to the team from day one. With the other one, I couldn't so much picture that. I made a specific video where I break down the formula for the bullet points more in detail. I'll link it somewhere up here. Quick break. If you want more videos like this on job search, LinkedIn, and how to move up in your career, hit subscribe so you don't miss out on the next one. I post regularly on topics like this. Now, let's get into what actually matters more than your resume right now. Here's something that most people get backwards. Yes, of course, your resume still needs to be solid, but your LinkedIn profile is super important right now for two reasons. First, this is increasingly how recruiters look for candidates instead of you chasing them. If your profile is optimized with the right headline, keywords, photo, experience section, and so on, if you're being clear online about the value that you give to businesses, recruiters will start coming to your inbox instead of your resume getting buried under a thousand other ones. Second, even if a recruiter sees your resume first, they are almost always going to check you out on LinkedIn as well. Just to form an impression and see that your claims on the resume actually match up with what you're saying online. It's a credibility background check. So, if your resume is strong, but your LinkedIn is half-finished or outdated, you're undoing your own work. Optimize both. But, if you only have time for one thing this week, make it LinkedIn. 87% of recruiters say that LinkedIn is the best way to vet a candidate's background. I personally got my last job by reaching out to a hiring manager directly through LinkedIn. Before that, I thoroughly optimized my profile to communicate and position myself exactly in a way that was needed for that role. So, please don't underestimate the power of LinkedIn. In addition to that, I started getting active on LinkedIn by commenting and posting on industry experts' posts, and since then, I have at least five recruiters in my inbox every single month. So, I can tell you it works. One final tip, if there's a role that you really want where you think, "Okay, this is my dream job. I definitely am a good match for this." Go above and beyond. Do something that makes you memorable, something that makes you stand out. Record a short video introducing yourself. Put together a small mini project specifically for that company, something that shows that you already thought about their problems before they're even ever interviewing you. When I applied for my role in banking, I did exactly that. I attached a mini slide deck detailing the problems that I saw at the company was facing and then aligned out approaches and strategies of how to tackle them. It made me stand out from other candidates and eventually landed me the job. This is now more relevant than ever as the number of applications and candidates that you're competing with has increased and thus you need real differentiators to stand out. A well-positioned and optimized LinkedIn profile, a resume including the five updates we just talked about in line with your profile, and a means to stand out whether that's a slide deck, a video, or any other short document that speaks to the company's problems. And of course, going above and beyond and making a whole slide deck on tackling a certain problem, I would only do that and recommend that for a position that you really want because it takes a lot of time but it's worth the return in the end compared to mass sending out generic applications like everyone who has optimized their resume with ChatGPT or Claude these days. To recap, swap your address for your LinkedIn profile URL, add a tailored key accomplishments or executive summary section at the top of your resume. Prioritize relevant roles over listing every single position you ever held. Use scannable bullet points over dense paragraphs and show impact, not just the tasks that you were responsible for. Then, take it a step further and optimize your LinkedIn. Go above and beyond with extra material if you're applying for a role that you really, really want. If you found this helpful, hit the like button, subscribe if you haven't already, and let me know in the comments which one of these you're updating first. Thanks for watching. I'll see you in the next video.

transcript: Most PMs use AI to write faster, but the ones who are getting promoted are using it for eight things that you're probably not. With new AI tools popping up left and right, it can be overwhelming to know when it makes sense to use AI in project management to increase productivity and in which situations it ends up wasting more of your time than it saves you. In this video, [clears throat] I'll break down the eight best use cases for using AI in project management and which tools to use to put you ahead of 99% of project managers out there. Let's get into it. One quick note before we start. For a lot of you, your company's IT policy will restrict which tools you can use anyways, and that's totally normal. So, this video is less about which exact tool to download today and more about the use case itself. Also, once you can show your manager a clear before and after, for example, how many hours a specific use case has saved you, that's the strongest argument for getting a new tool approved anyways, if you need it. Now, of course, AI is not going to replace you as a project manager. It's not built for that complex human side of the job, the difficult conversations, the politics, the judgment calls. That's still up to you. But, what it is obviously very good at is automating the admin-heavy, repetitive tasks, the ones that can end up eating 30 to 40% of your week. So, in essence, AI can help project managers freeing up time to focus on what matters, the more important strategic side of things. That being said, let's see how AI can support you in the day-to-day. Use case number one, project planning. Let's start at the beginning with project planning because this is where a lot of project managers waste time without realizing it. When I was leading a $3 million project for an investment app at a bank, the hardest part in week one wasn't the strategy. It was translating a vague business goal into an actual structured roadmap, a project plan with work streams, milestones, dependencies that 15 cross-functional stakeholders could actually align on. And this is exactly where AI earns its place today. Tools like ClickUp Brain and Asana AI can take a rough project brief or paragraph that you type in or you dictate and turn it into a structured task breakdown that can then be turned into a structured roadmap project plan with clear owners within minutes. Also, if your organization allows general assistance like Claude or ChatGPT, you can feed those LLMs your project charters, your objectives, your constraints, and all the other project documents and ask it to draft a first outline of your project plan. Now, I want to be clear here. The AI output is always only a first draft. You are still the one who understands the constraints, the politics, and your specific stakeholders. But, going from a completely blank page to an 80% draft of your project plan, that is a real use case. The refining then obviously still comes from you. Use case number two, resource management. Now, for the second use case, we're going to be looking at resource and capacity planning. We all know that this is not a new problem that AI suddenly invented a new method for. Sprint planning, capacity spreadsheets, Jira boards, and so on. So, the issue wasn't that we didn't have a method to plan the capacity of our teams as a project manager. It's more that all of it was manual, and manual means that it eats up time, and it's only ever as current as the last time someone updated it. If you have ever managed a team where three people are quietly overbooked and nobody catches it until the deadline is already slipping, that can get really messy. And again, this is where AI can really change something. Tools like monday.com and Wrike now have AI-powered workload views, which update in real time so that you can see who's over capacity and who still has room without anyone having to manually type it in. And for a bigger multi-project environments, tools like Epicflow go even a step further. They have predictive capacity modeling, which can flag resource conflicts months before they're happening across your whole portfolio and not just one project. So, the job hasn't changed. Resource planning was always a part of project management, but what changed is the lag with which it automate and the time that is needed to update it. On a private banking digital transformation project that I was working on, I was managing a team of 20 stakeholders who were both internal and external and widely spread across departments. And I was doing exactly that kind of capacity planning but manually or using Jira for example. Having these kind of AI tools would have saved me hours every week. Use case three, email management. I think this one doesn't get talked about enough but realistically having to answer emails to stakeholders and everyone inside your company can eat up to three to four hours each week for a project manager. title: The Project Manager Promotion Strategy | How to Get Noticed at Work
description:
Always being overlooked when it comes to promotions?

You've delivered projects on time, managed difficult stakeholders, and held your team together under pressure — and yet someone with less experience just got the senior role you were expecting. That's not a coincidence. That's a visibility problem.

The uncomfortable truth? The people making promotion decisions often don't know what you're capable of. Your line manager knows. But the executives two levels above you — the ones sitting in the rooms where those decisions actually happen — likely don't. And that is something you can change, starting today.

In this video, I'm sharing 4 concrete strategies to build your visibility with the right people inside your organization. This isn't office politics. It's career management — a skill most project managers were never taught, but every senior PM needs. What I cover:

 Why outstanding delivery alone won't get you promoted
 How to apply stakeholder mapping to your own career (not just your projects)
 The counterintuitive way to get direct access to senior leaders
 Why most PMs unknowingly give away credit for their own results — and how to stop
 The low-effort LinkedIn habit that puts you on the radar of decision-makers inside and beyond your org

 TIMESTAMPS
00:00 - Intro 
00:28 - Tip No. 1: Stakeholder Mapping 
02:20 - Tip No. 2: Voluntary Initiatives 
03:18 - Tip No. 3: Presenting Results Directly 
04:11 - Tip No. 4: LinkedIn Executive Engagement 
05:56 - Final Thoughts  

 Want to build your own visibility strategy? I offer free 30-minute discovery calls where we map your specific situation and define your next steps. https://calendly.com/larahadry521/30min

transcript: You have to deliver projects on time, manage difficult stakeholders, you've held teams together under pressure, and you hit your milestones. But, you are still waiting for the promotion that should have come by now. Someone with less experience just got the senior role you were expecting, and that is not coincidence. The problem is not your delivery, it's not your skill. The people making the promotion decisions, they simply don't know what you are capable of. And that is something that you can change starting today. Tip number one, map your internal stakeholders like a project. Now, every project manager knows how to map project stakeholders. You identify who has influence, who makes decisions, and who needs to be kept informed at all times, and who can potentially also block your progress. But, your career path stakeholders, too. And most project managers have never met them. You should start by asking yourself, who are the leaders in my organization who influence promotion decisions? Not just your direct manager, the executives two levels above you. The people who sit in the rooms where those conversations really happen. Now, the next question you should ask is, which of those people actually know what I'm working on? Which of them could speak to my capabilities if they were asked? For most project managers, the answer is not many people. But, once you have that map, you can look at where you already have connections. For example, a colleague who works very closely with a senior leader. Where you don't have a connection yet, go direct. So, this is something most people never do because it feels uncomfortable. But, reaching out to a senior leader for a 30-minute conversation, not to ask for anything, but to learn from them, to understand their priorities, to introduce yourself, especially if you're new to the organization, this is one of the most underused career tools that a project manager can have. I did this early in my banking career. I wanted to get in front of a specific board member, so I mapped who I already had known, found a senior executive that I had never spoken to before, and I reached out directly. She told me she was really pleasantly surprised because not a lot of people on the level that I was at, like quite junior, would normally do that. Now, that relationship led me to joining a voluntary initiative that she was sponsoring. Six months later, I was invited to an exclusive talent lunch with this board member. And shortly after this, I was handed to lead a 3 million euro project. Tip number two, get in the room through voluntary initiatives. Once you know who the decision makers are, you should look for ways to work alongside them. Most organizations have voluntary initiatives, like working groups, task force, or cross-functional programs that sit outside of the formal structure. For example, sustainability committees, innovation sprints, or even a graduate mentoring program. And these are almost always sponsored by senior leaders, and they're almost always under-subscribed because most people are too focused, obviously, on their daily job and putting out fires here and there to even raise their hand for any kind of voluntary side initiative. Now, raising your hand costs you a few hours a month, but what it gives you is direct, repeated exposure to the people that would otherwise never interact with. Now, you're someone they have worked with. They have seen perform under pressure, and they have chosen to trust with something that they actually care about. That is a completely different starting position when a senior role opens up. Tip number three, present your results directly to leadership. This one is simple, but most project managers never do it. When a project wraps up or hits a significant milestone, most project managers hand the results to the line manager and move on to the next thing. The line manager then presents it upwards, and the credit travels with the message, not the person who actually did the work. So, start asking for the opportunity to present directly, even if you're still rather junior. It does not need to be a big moment. A 5-minute slot in a leadership team meeting or a short summary is directly to the relevant senior stakeholder. Now, this does two things. It puts your name and your face in front of the people who matter, and it signals something about who you are as a project manager. You're someone who takes ownership of the outcomes, who can communicate clearly to a senior audience, and who is thinking beyond the task in front of them. Tip number four, engage with executives on LinkedIn. Most senior leaders are now building a presence on LinkedIn. They're posting about strategy, leadership, about what they are working on. And the comment section on those posts is almost always full of generic responses that say nothing. A thoughtful, specific comment on an executive's LinkedIn post puts your name in front of them in a context that is completely separate from your day-to-day role. And it shows that you are engaged with ideas beyond your immediate project. It shows you can communicate with clarity and confidence. And it's not just the executive who sees it. Their entire network does. Recruiters, hiring managers, senior project managers across your industry, they are all reading those posts, too. This applies whether the executive is inside your organization or not. If there is a leader in the field whose thinking you actually, honestly respect, engaging with that content consistently is a very low-effort way to stay on their radar all the time. transcript: Are you new to project management or thinking about breaking in? For example, the bank that I worked for wanted customers to use their mobile banking app more often. So, they started a project. Before any work starts on a project, you need to understand what the business actually wants. What are the businesses goals with that specific project? That's what requirement gathering is, basically. You can think of it like a wish list. You go around to everyone who has a stake in the project. So, for example, you're asking customers, you're going to ask your manager, you're going to ask different team members. And you go to them and you ask, "What do you need? What problem are we trying to solve with this project? What would a good outcome look like for you?" And certain decisions, like anything touching security, compliance, legal, that needed an actual sign-off from the legal and risk team specifically, and that was very well documented in the project governance. Moving on to number six, the steering committee. A steering committee is a group of senior people, executives, usually leaders that come from different parts of the business, who oversee the project from above. They don't really do the day-to-day work on the project, but their job is to make the big calls, the big decisions, while making sure that the project is overall always aligned with the business goals. Their roles and accountabilities are also documented in the project governance that we talked about previously. Now, for example, in my project, it looked like this. My steering committee included the head of product, the CTO, and the head of customer experience. We met twice a month and I, as a project manager, presented where things stood. I flagged anything that needed a decision above my level, and I included a recommendation based on my analysis, and they then either approve or redirect. Now, if you see steering committee reporting in a job description, this is what they mean. You'll be the one preparing those updates and running those meetings to mainly senior executives in the organization. Moving on to number seven, the kickoff meeting. Now, the governance is set up, the scope is agreed, you have all of the requirements gathered together, and it's officially time to start. That's what the kickoff is for. A kickoff meeting is the official first meeting of the project. It's the moment where everyone who's involved, all all the stakeholders who have a stake in the project, they come together for the first time to align on what the project is, why it matters, who is doing what, and how the team will actually work together. It sets the tone for everything that follows. In my banking project, I ran a kickoff with the full project team, with the developers, designers, the testers, the product owner, and all of the other key stakeholders and executives from the business that were involved. Together we then walked through the project goals, the project scope, the timeline, and the governance that we had agreed on. By the end of that meeting, everyone in the room knew exactly what we were doing and what their role was. Number eight, risk management. This is another term that you'll likely read in one of the PM job descriptions. Now, for risk management, the project manager's job is to look ahead and spot problems before they actually happen. Risk management in its core is the process of identifying things that could go wrong, deciding how likely they're are actually going to happen, and then making a plan for what you would do if things actually went wrong. Now, what could that look like? One risk on my project was that adding new features to the app could somehow breach the security of the customer's data, which would then mean both damage to the customers, of course, as well as potential fines and also reputation loss for the bank as a whole. Because we were changing so much in the app, that risk was actually quite likely to happen, and the impacts would have been severe. So, from day one, we involved the bank's security and compliance team directly in the project. They reviewed every feature design before the development even started, and we had a mandatory sign-off checkpoint built into the timeline. So, nothing could launch without their green light. We also made sure that all new features followed the existing data protection standards that the bank already had in place. Those were some of the risk mitigating actions that we had planned and documented in the risk register beforehand. This way, we're prepared for the worst. Now, luckily, this risk never actually became an issue, but that's exactly the point. Because even if it would have done, we would have had a plan to mitigate it and to do damage control early on. Term number nine, change request. Now, even the best planned projects sometimes get asked to change direction. And a change request is the formal way that this happens. A change request is basically an official ask to change something about the project like the scope, the timeline, the budget, or the way something is being built. And the keyword is official. Instead of someone just verbally going, "Oh, can we maybe add this?" A change request makes this formal. It documents the impact of this change and it requires proper approval, mostly from the steering committee, before anything can change. So, for example, halfway through my banking project, the marketing team came to me and they said, "Hey, we want to add a referral program feature to the app because we've seen it with competitors and it's working really well." Now, this was clearly something that wasn't in the original scope. So, I raised a formal change request. I documented what it would require to implement this extra feature. So, we would, for example, need two extra developers. We would need three additional weeks. Then the steering committee reviewed the change request and they decided that the feature was worth it. They approved the extra resource and we updated the plan and got going. Now, that's how it should work. There's no surprises, no chaos, just a clear decision. And finally, number 10, the status report. A status report is a regular update, usually weekly or bi-weekly, that tells everyone involved in the project how things are actually going. Are we on track? Are we on budget? Has anything been completed yet? Are there any bottlenecks or risks that have been flagged? It keeps both the steering committee and the key stakeholders and the project team informed without them needing to attend every single meeting or chase the project manager for updates so they know what's actually going on. So, for example, again in my app project, every Friday I would send a one-page status report to the steering committee and to the senior stakeholders. Green meant that everything was on track, amber meant there was something to watch, and red meant we had a problem that needed a fast decision. That simple traffic light system meant that even people who weren't in the day-to-day and weren't super informed about the status of the project could still see at a glance where things stood. For this, I personally like to keep it simple and just give it two to three sentences on each relevant area of the project to describe the status, describe a risk, or describe the next action. So, if a job description mentions stakeholder reporting or project status updates, this is exactly what that means. So, there you have it. 10 project management terms with a real example behind every single one. To recap the order we went through, you start with understanding what a project is, then you gather all of the requirements to understand what you're building and what the goal of that project is. You define the scope to put a boundary around what is inside and what is outside of the project, and then you agree on certain deliverables that you will produce. You set up a governance so that everyone knows who decides what. You establish a steering committee for the big calls, including all of the executives and maybe board members. Then you hold a kickoff meeting for the project where you bring everyone into a virtual or a physical actual room and get everyone on the same page about the project. What is also part of a project is managing the risks before they actually become problems, and when certain things come up and your project needs a change, then you put in a formal change request, which is then approved by the steering committee before you can move on with actually implementing those changes. Finally, you keep everyone involved in the project through regular status reports. And now, when you read those words in the job description, I hope it became a little bit clearer what they're actually asking for. If there's a project management term you've come across that still confuses you, drop it in the comments and I'll have a look at it and reply to you as soon as possible. Thank you so much for watching. If you found this helpful at all, give it a like, subscribe for more content like this, and I'll see you in the next video.

title: Project Manager Interview Questions and Answers (2026 Guide)

transcript: If you want to break into project management, you need to know that the process is not the same as for any other office role. There's a certain structure and several different rounds in which the hiring managers expect the candidates to respond in a specific way. Now, I know this can seem daunting if you've never done it before. But to make sure you ace your interview, you need to prepare accordingly. In this video, we'll look at the four different stages of a PM interview. We'll look at different interview questions that I had to solve during my own PM interviews and how to answer them in detail. Let's get into it. The PM interview process is usually structured into four different stages, depending on the size of the company. The first stage is the HR screening interview. Usually, you would go through an HR screening interview first, which can be a call or a meeting from anywhere between 15 to 30 minutes. Here, the recruiter is vetting your baseline qualifications as well as your overall cultural fit to the company. This step of the process is similar to other positions. Recruiters usually have a checklist from the hiring manager, where if the role requires specific years of experience or certain certifications, this is the moment the recruiter verifies this with you. So, be ready to confirm certain years of experience, a certain methodology, or a certain certification like the CAPM that you might have done. At this stage, when they ask you cultural questions, just keep your answers short and punchy because this is just a high-level check. In addition, they might ask you for your salary expectation not to waste anyone's time just in case there's a big mismatch. To prepare for this, you can just research the market rate of a PM with your experience level in 2026. If they ask you, you can say, "Based on the responsibilities of this role and the current market, I'm looking for a range of X to Y, but I'm flexible depending on the total benefits package." Don't state a concrete number here just yet because they might nail you down on it. Instead, give a range and discuss the final amount in later interview rounds. And lastly, in this stage, they might ask you about the logistics, so your earliest possible start date or relocation requirements and so on. My advice, be honest here. If they're looking for a candidate to come come the office three times a week and you want a 100% remote position or they want you to relocate and you cannot because you have family responsibilities. It's better to find out now. The second stage, the behavioral questions. In the second round, they will most likely be testing your behavior and communication skills. In my previous interviews, this was a 60-minute interview with the hiring manager as well as a senior project manager from the team. As project management fundamentally is people management, most likely what they will be testing here is your emotional intelligence, your communication as well as your social interaction skills. Now, let's go over five very common questions and how to answer them properly. What matters most here is how you answer the questions. You don't just want to ramble on without a structure or a clear start and end point. To answer the questions in a structured way, you can use the STAR method. S stands for situation. So, you want to first of all explain what is happening. Then you move on to T, the task. So, identify the task at hand that evolves from the situation. A for action. So, what would you do in this given situation? And then you end with R, what is the eventual result? Let's see how this could look like based on an actual interview question that I had. Question number one, how do you handle conflict within your project team? Here they're looking to evaluate your emotional intelligence. You want to demonstrate that you move the conversation away from who is right to what is actually best for the project. You aren't the judge. You're the person who brings the right tools and methods to the table so that the team can reach consensus themselves. Try and find a situation from your previous job or your studies where you actually demonstrated how you handled conflict even if that was not in the project management context. Using the STAR method, start with the situation. For example, let's say you worked in a customer service role and this is the given situation. Our call center's quality assurance lead and our supervisors were in a heated disagreement. Quality assurance wanted longer scripted calls to ensure 100% accuracy while supervisors wanted shorter calls to reduce the wait queue. Now, you presented the interviewers with the conflict situation. What was the task at hand for you? I needed to facilitate a resolution because the tension was causing confusion for the agents and hurting our overall performance metrics. What did you do in order to solve it? I acted as a neutral facilitator, shifting the debate from opinions to user data. I pulled reports showing that after the 5-minute mark, customer satisfaction dropped regardless of accuracy. I proposed a pilot for a hybrid script that prioritized the most critical data points first. By centering the conversation on customer impact rather than internal quotas, the team reached a consensus. And finally, what was the outcome? We implemented the hybrid flow. Average handle time dropped by 45 seconds and our QA scores actually improved because the scripts were more focused. Question number three, how do you handle difficult or disengaged stakeholders? This tests your people management skills. Here your answer should show that you can tailor your communication. Don't treat a CFO the same way you treat a lead developer in your communication. Show the interviewer that first you identify what keeps that stakeholder up at night, whether that's ROI or legal compliance or security risk, and then adjust your reporting to address those concerns. Let's say you worked in marketing previously and a specific situation that you can give as an example to this answer could be this. During a 2026 rebranding campaign, our head of legal became a major bottleneck. He was skeptical of our new community-driven social strategy, fearing it opened the brand too much to liability, and he eventually stopped responding to our creative approval requests. What did you have to do in that case? I had to re-engage him to avoid a hard block on our launch date as we couldn't go live without his department's sign-off. Okay, then what did you do? I tailored my communication to his specific concerns. Instead of sending him creative decks and vibe boards, I created a weekly compliance and risk dashboard. This report highlighted the specific moderation tools and community guidelines we had built to mitigate risk. I also invited him to a beta test of our response protocol. By speaking his language of liability and protection, I turned his skepticism into active collaboration. And what was the result? He became our biggest advocate on the executive board. And his input helped us create a pre-approved content library that sped up our future campaign launches by 40%. Question number four, describe a moment of success and how you achieved it. Here they want to see that you can understand that success means having an actual business impact or adding value to a business and not just finishing a task. Because many candidates here make the mistake of saying the project was a success because we managed to finish on time. To a hiring manager that just means you're doing your job. A great answer connects your work to the company success. Did you increase revenue? Did you improve user retention? Did you save any costs? As another example how to answer this question, let's say that your background was in recruiting. In early 2025, our company was struggling to scale our engineering department. We had a high volume of applicants, but only 2% were making it through the final interview stage. What was your task here? My task was to increase the offer acceptance rate while reducing the time to hire. As the long delay was causing us to lose top-tier to faster competitors. So, what did you do? I led a process audit and identified a major friction point. A redundant technical screening that took five days to grade. I coordinated with the engineering leads to replace it with a real-time collaborative coding session. By streamlining the funnel and implementing an automated scheduling tool, I transformed a four-week hiring cycle into a 10-day experience for the candidate. What's the result? The bottom line or the so what for the company? This led to a 60% increase in offer acceptance and saved the engineering team 20 hours of interview time per month. Question number five, how do you prioritize tasks to meet deadlines? Here the interviewer wants to hear that you have a repeatable logic for making choices. They don't just want to hear I picked the most important thing. Here it's best to name drop certain frameworks like Eisenhower matrix or the MoSCoW framework to show that you can make an objective data-based prioritization and choice rather than just going with who's screaming the loudest. For this question, let's say you come from a background in the creative industry and you want to again give a specific example of how you handle the prioritization of tasks. So, what's the situation? In my role as a creative lead, I was hit with 30-plus simultaneous requests from minor social media edits to a high-stakes website redesign, all with conflicting ASAP deadlines. What did you have to do? I had to decide which tasks would actually drive our launch goals and which were just noise that would distract the team from delivering on time. What did you do? I applied the Eisenhower matrix to categorize the backlog. I sat down with the department heads to separate what was urgent and important, like fixing a broken checkout button, from what was merely urgent but not important, like a last-minute request for an internal slide deck. By visualizing the work this way, I was able to delegate the minor tasks and ruthlessly deprioritize projects that didn't align with our quarterly growth metrics. What was the result? We delivered the five highest-impact projects on time. This resulted in a 25% jump in user engagement during launch week and I reduced the team's overtime by 15% because we stopped chasing low-value distractions. These are very common questions that you might be asked in a PM interview, but don't be scared because you can write down your answers to these questions before you get to the interview using the STAR method, learn it, prepare it, practice it with other people so that you come prepared to the interview and know what to say. Because it's very unlikely that in a stressful situation, you will just come up with all of these situations on the spot. So, come prepared. Once you made it through stage one and two of the PM interview process, you're going to move to the third stage, the case study. This is the part where most people get really nervous. It can either be a 60-minute in-person interview or a 48-hour take-home assignment. Here, the company isn't just looking for the right answer. They're looking for your process. They want to see how you tackle a real-world messy problem and put it in a structured way without spiraling. Personally, for case studies, I usually use a shorter revised version of the STAR method, which you can also use alternatively. I call it the SCS framework. It's the situation, the challenge, and the solution. So, first of all, I rephrase the situation given to me in my own words to make sure that I understood it. Then, I'll identify the core challenge, and finally present the interviewers with a solution that I came up with. It's punchy, fast, and it keeps you from rambling in an unstructured way. Let's look at a case that I actually had to solve, but keep in mind this is more for a mid to senior PM role. For me, this was a take-home assignment, which I had 48 hours to solve, and I had to prepare a short slide deck to present my ideas. The case was, "A traditional bank wants to digitalize their product offer to be more attractive to Gen Z customers within a strict 6-month window. How would you structure a project to achieve this?" Using my SCS framework, situation, challenge, solution, on the first slide, I rephrased the situation from my own point of view. So, if I understand this correctly, we're looking at a traditional bank that needs to pivot fast to capture a younger demographic, Gen Z customers, who expect a seamless mobile-first experience. We have a hard 6-month deadline to go from traditional to digital-ready without breaking any regulations. If they ask you to prepare a short slide deck for this, or even if they don't, but it's a take-home assignment, and you want to make a good impression, then it's best to actually prepare some slides. You can simply use an AI tool, and help you visualize this kind of quote into different graphics using screenshots, statistics, and so on, to make it visually more appealing than just putting text on a slide. What I added here to rephrasing the situation that they gave me was, for example, the context of Gen Z wanting seamless and mobile-first experience. Also, given the context of banking, I added that we needed to make all of this project come true within the given boundaries of regulations, as banking is a very regulated industry. Then, I went on to iterate the challenge. The real challenge here isn't just building an app. It's the speed to market versus security trade-off. We need to make sure we hit the market fast so we can compete with our fintech competitors while also navigating the slow-moving world of the banking compliance. If we move too slow, we risk losing the market and our potential first-mover advantage. If we move too fast and have a security breach, we do not only risk the bank's reputation, but we also risk getting big signs. Now comes the main part, the solution. Here I detail my structured approach to this project. In the initiation phase, I would set up a business case to map budget of the project. I would include a risk assessment and document it in a log. And finally, I would meant stakeholder responsibilities using a RACI matrix. Then, I would structure this project into four parallel work streams and define major milestones along the six-month project roadmap. The potential for work streams, for example, could be stream one, compliance and legal. We start this on day one because it's the longest lead time and the foundation of our work. Stream two, UX and UI design, focusing specifically on features that Gen Z actually want. Stream three, technical infrastructure, using a mobile middleware approach so we don't have to rebuild the entire bank's core back end just to launch an app. Stream four, marketing. Make sure to include the marketing team to plan a campaign around our launch, mainly on our socials to reach our audience. Then I would also include what kind of key milestones I would define along the six-month roadmap. For example, key milestone one could be stakeholder and legal alignment. This is where we get the green light from the legal and compliance teams on the core concept so we don't hit any roadblocks halfway through. Milestone two, feature prioritization and UX freeze. So we take all that customer feedback, figure out which three to five features actually move the needle, and lock it in the designs so the developers can start building. Milestone three, MVP development and technical sync. This is the heavy lifting phase where the core product is built and we ensure all the different systems and APIs are actually talking to each other. Milestone four, marketing content and beta prep. While the developers are squashing bugs, we're getting the marketing plan, landing pages, and how-to content ready for our first group of beta testers. Milestone five, the big bang launch and review. We push the product live to the public, monitor the data, and then sit down as a team to figure out what worked, what didn't work, and what we're building next. Lastly, I also want to mention the methodology I would propose to use during this 6-month project. I would use an agile method and work in 2-week sprints to make sure we get the speed while integrating potentially changing customer needs along the way. We have several different check-ins scheduled along the road map with the project team and sponsor to integrate feedback and make sure we can discuss any bottlenecks. This approach shows the hiring managers clearly that you know how to structure and approach a project. If you were to be hired the next day, and a situation like this actually came up, they would know, "Okay, we can put this person in charge, and they know how to do it, they know what steps to follow, and we can fully rely on them." Now, the fourth and final stage, the vibe check. As I mentioned in the beginning, the stages of the PM interview process depend also on the size of the company. So, for example, it could also be that you have another round in between where you talk to senior executives or the CEO, so they kind of want to get to know you. I'll make a separate video on this on how to answer interview questions with senior executives in the final round. More likely, and also in my case, I had a vibe check with the team. So, you've passed the technical part, they kind of know you can do the job, and now they want to know, "Is this person likable? Can we see ourselves working with them on a day-to-day?" This is usually a 30-to-45-minute call, for example, with other project managers or developers, UX leaders, marketers, and so on. For this stage, I'd recommend be yourself as much as possible. Take it easy. Don't try and come across as a know-it-all because it will just seem arrogant, but instead, come across as if you're genuinely interested in getting to know that other person. The PM interview process is a marathon, but if you stay structured, use frameworks, and prepare, practice, practice, practice, you will be fine. If you want more one-on-one guidance or have specific questions for your situation, you can book a free discovery call with me. I'll put the link in the description down below. Now, I hope this helps. Hit the like button. Let me know in the comments what you think about it, and subscribe to follow along for more content like this. You'll get that offer. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next video.

title: What I Wish I Knew Before Taking the PMI ACP Exam
description:
Nobody told me these things before I sat the PMI-ACP — and they almost cost me the pass.

Passing the PMI-ACP isn't just about knowing agile frameworks inside out. There are specific traps built into this exam that even well-prepared candidates fall into. I passed in three weeks — but not without running into 3 challenges. In this video I'm breaking down exactly what caught me off guard and what I did about it, so you don't have to figure it out the hard way.

What I cover:
 Why the "right" answer is often a trap — and how to think past it
 The time pressure problem nobody warns you about 
 One decision that could make or break your focus on exam day

If you're currently studying for the PMI-ACP or planning to sit it soon, watch this before you book your exam date.

transcript: I passed the PMI-ACP in 3 weeks working full-time and honestly, there were moments during that exam where I genuinely wasn't sure if I was going to make it or not. So, in this video, I want to be really honest with you about three things that I found the hardest and that I didn't see anyone else talk about when I was looking on YouTube for PMI-ACP content, so you can walk in better equipped than I was. Let's get into it. Okay, so the first thing that caught me off guard and I've heard this from many other people, too, is the best answer problem. Here's what I mean. Questions are multiple-choice, which is quite standard, but many of them can sound like they could be true. So, often all four options, especially for the scenario-based questions, they seem like valid Agile practices or they even are, but you must select the best option for that specific scenario that is being described. So, in that sense, memorizing a definition will only get you so far as the majority of the questions are those scenario-based questions where you really need to apply your own critical thinking and understanding of servant leadership. And that's the game. It's not testing whether you know the definition of Agile and servant leadership or what a retrospective is. It's testing whether you understand how to apply those concepts in a specific human situation. And that's where a lot of people, including myself, at certain points start second-guessing themselves. Is this the best possible answer? Is that actually what they want to hear? With the ACP, the trap is that you're reading scenarios about team dynamics, stakeholder relationships, conflict, and so on. And you have to go, "Okay, what does a genuinely good Agile project manager do in this given situation?" Not just what is technically correct. So, my honest advice, stop trying to memorize definitions. That will only get you so far. Focus on understanding the why behind Agile values. Why does a servant leader step back instead of step in? Why does a transparency matter more than efficiency in certain moments? When you understand the reasoning, the answer starts to become more obvious, even when all four options sometimes seem like they could be the best option. If you're unsure about a question, here's what I did. I first went through all of the options and looked at which one was definitely not the right one and strike it through. They have a strike through option in the exam. And then I marked the question to come back later to with a clearer mind and make a final decision on the best option. Now, the second thing I found really hard about the exam was the time pressure because a lot of the practice exams that I had done before, they had quite short answers and short questions making it really likely to get through all of the exam in a short amount of time, definitely 3 hours. But the actual exam questions and answers both entailed way more words. They were way longer and it took much more time to actually read through them. So believe it or not, these 3 hours actually go by so quickly. You see the timer in the right upper corner counting down adding to your stress. What helped me here was using the highlighter function. I used it to highlight the core part of each question and not get lost in all of the surrounding words to be able to answer them more efficiently. Use the highlighter to mark all of the relevant words, to mark what actually is the essence of the question, and to maybe also highlight those answer options that you think might be best suitable for the specific question. The third thing about this exam that I found quite challenging was the technical setup. Because I decided to take the test online at home and I was really not 100% sure whether my Wi-Fi was going to turn off unexpectedly or whether in the rush of it all I accidentally moved too far out of the screen which would actually result in the examiner thinking I'm cheating and me actually eventually failing the exam. And I didn't even dare to go to the toilet in the designated break because I thought, "Okay, maybe then I come back too late or something happens in the meantime with the technical setup or the Wi-Fi and everything breaks apart." And I really didn't want to risk that. In the end I also wasn't sure if after all those 3 hours hitting that button would actually submit my whole exam correctly or not. So my tip here, if you have a very old laptop or not the best most stable Wi-Fi, you should consider doing the test at a test center just to save you the nerves of potential technical failure. The point is, industry context matters, and it should shape your decision about which direction you actually want to go. But given all of that, what should you actually do? If you're not sure what kind of work or industry you want to go into, or you're just open to any kind of different industry and role because you're just want to increase your chances of actually landing a job, I would recommend to start with the project manager path.
