title: This 2-Minute "Tell Me About Yourself" Formula Lands More Job Offers in 2026 (+IRL examples)
description:
Are you struggling to answer “Tell Me About Yourself” in a job interview?
This is one of the most common interview questions — and also the one that causes most candidates to fail.

Often, candidates simply give a chronological timeline of their resume. There is a much better approach that top tier candidates use to convince the hiring managers. 

In this video, I'll cover:
Why the traditional "chronological" resume summary is killing your chances in the 2026 market.
The neurobiology of storytelling and how to use oxytocin to build instant trust with hiring managers.
A deep dive into the 3-Step Magic Formula (Challenge, Transformation, Result) to structure your "Tell Me About Yourself" answer.
Two word-for-word examples responses using the formula in action 

The "brutal" job market of 2026 demands more than just a list of degrees and keywords. When an interviewer asks, "Tell me about yourself," they aren't looking for a verbal recital of your LinkedIn profile—they are looking for a reason to keep listening.

In this video, I break down why average applicants bore the room while elite candidates use the Hero’s Journey to command it. We explore how to establish your "professional spark," frame your experience through high-stakes conflict, and demonstrate a transformation that proves your unique selling proposition (USP). 

You’ll learn how to stop being a list of dates and start being the hero who solves the company’s specific problems. Whether you are a seasoned executive or a career switcher, this framework will help you own the first two minutes of the interview and set a tone of authority and competence for the rest of the conversation.

 Timestamps:
00:00 – Introduction: The Crucial First Impression 
00:33 – Critical Mistakes to Avoid
01:19 – The 3-Step Magic Formula  
02:11 – Step 1: The Challenge 
03:03 – Step 2: The Transformation 
03:21 – Step 3: The Result  
04:02 – Sample Answer 1
05:49 – Sample Answer 2
07:48 – Final Tips 

Work With Me
Ready to master your specific story? Let’s refine your "Magic Formula" together so you can walk into your next interview with total confidence.  https://calendly.com/larahadry521/30min

 You'll also like
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e3hRVUrbd7A&t=19s 

#InterviewTips #CareerAdvice #TellMeAboutYourself #JobSearch2026 #InterviewPrep #Storytelling #CareerGrowth #Hiring2026
transcript: You finally landed an interview in this brutal job market. But, the clock is already ticking. Most candidates lose their job offer within the first 120 seconds. You think you're just introducing yourselves, but in reality, you're being filtered out before the real conversation even starts. With just one answer, your chances are gone. Average applicants bore the room by summarizing their resume. Top tier candidates use a strategic storytelling formula to command the room. Today, I'm breaking down the three step magic formula that forces the hiring manager to pay attention and makes you the only logical choice. Let's be honest. If you answer, "Tell me about yourself." with a chronological play-by-play, "In 2015, I did my bachelor's, then I started my master's, then I started working at this and this company." You are making three critical mistakes. First, you are boring the interviewers. You're making them do the work of finding what's interesting about you, and they will lose attention fast. Second, you don't stand out. Every candidate is giving pretty much the same timeline as you. Third, and most importantly, you're showing that you cannot tell a story. You're proving that you cannot filter the noise and find what actually matters. In 2026, being a great communicator and knowing how to structure your answer matters more than ever. This first impression sets the tone for the rest of the interview. Instead, you need storytelling. Humans are neurologically wired for stories. When we hear a well-told narrative, our brains release oxytocin, the feel-good hormone, that builds empathy and trust. To do this, we use a framework that's called the hero's journey. Most great stories follow this formula. There's a hero that is undergoing a challenge. They're having a transformative moment, and they come out on the other side as a result of it. Think about Cinderella. She's the hero, or the main character. Her challenge is that she lives under her stepmom's thumb as a servant, and she really wants to attend the royal ball. Her transformation happens through magical help to attend a ball in a beautiful dress with beautiful shoes. As a result, she marries a prince and becomes royalty herself. Now, you're not going to talk about Cinderella. Although, this would also be quite memorable. But, instead, you're going to use this exact same structure to talk about your professional life. Here's the three-step framework to make you unforgettable. As a foundation, you need to establish the hero. Don't just start with your job title, but start with your professional spark. Why are you obsessed with this field? It should be a short, personal truth that connects your personality to the job. If you're a developer, maybe it's your obsession with solving puzzles. If you're in HR, maybe you've always been fascinated by people dynamics. This makes you human and immediately builds this oxytocin-driven trust. Now, step one, the challenge. Start with the problem. This is where you introduce the hero, so yourself, in a conflict context. Every job, in one way or another, exists to solve a certain problem. By starting like this, you immediately establish yourself as a problem-solver. Describe a moment where the stakes were high, resources were low, or the path forward was unclear. This creates immediate tension and hooks the interviewers' curiosity. Step number two, the transformation. This is the how. It's the bridge between the challenge and the result. In this step, you describe the specific action you took, and more importantly, how you changed or what you've learned because of it. Did you have to master a new technology within a week, or did you have to learn how to lead a team through a crisis? Step three, the result. Finally, you deliver the payoff. You're releasing the tension that you have built with your story. What was the concrete outcome? You aren't just a candidate with experience. You are a person that has been tested and came out the other end with a superpower that this company needs. You share the concrete result, and then you do something that most candidates don't do. You turn that result into a system. You explain that the success of this project wasn't just a one-time lucky thing. It became your blueprint, the way you now approach every problem. Finally, you bring it all together by showing how your specific experience is the only logical solution to the company's current challenges. Example number one. Let's say you're a project manager. Here's what I would say when they ask me, "Tell me about yourself." So, a bit about myself, I've always been that person who's been pathologically organized. Even as a teenager, I was the one who would map out the most efficient route on trips with my friends. So, 5 years ago, I got into project management because I've always been driven to close the gap between a great idea and actually reaching your destination. And I realized early on that even in companies, many ideas fail because people don't follow through on something. That obsession with the gap was put to the test when after only 1 year as a management trainee at a global bank, I was asked to lead a $3 million investment app project. I was 24 years old stepping into a room with board members who had been in finance longer than I'd been alive. And I was responsible for leading the bank's number two priority for the entire year. I then realized very quickly that no amount of project tools or spreadsheets could save a project if the stakeholders didn't play along. I had to transform from a task tracker to a room reader. I learned that project management isn't about software or reporting, it's about psychology. It's about people. One year later, the app launched as the number one investment app in the German market. But more importantly, I walked away with a repeatable framework and understanding of navigating corporate complexity. I've spent the last years applying that same human-first logic to various industries and consulting. And I'm here today because I don't just meet deadlines. I move people to get the vision across the finish line. And I'm excited to do exactly that as a project manager here at XYZ. Then ideally, end your story with a question to create a conversation vibe and keep the interviewers engaged. For example, I love turning chaos into order like I did with that app launch. Where is the most friction in your projects right now? And what are you looking for in a project lead to come in and smooth that out? Let's look at a different example and role. Let's say you're in customer success. Here's how you can apply that formula if you're in a more client-facing, high-tech kind of role. I grew up in a family of small business owners, so I saw firsthand of what it means buying a solution that ends up creating more problems. I got into customer success because I hate seeing people feeling tricked by sales. I wanted to be the person who actually delivers on the promise made on the website. I took that philosophy with me when I started at a software-as-a-service startup that was losing 20% of its enterprise clients every quarter. I was handed our largest account, a client that was literally days away from canceling a six-figure contract. They were angry, they felt ignored, and they were ready to walk. Instead of apologizing for the software, I went and I spent three weeks on-site with them to figure out what their actual problem with the software was. I realized that the software itself was fine, but the team was using it in a way that was doubling their workload. I had to pivot from being a customer rep to becoming an internal consultant. I re-engineered their entire workflow and taught them how to use the tool and save two hours of manual input every day. The client didn't just stay, but they actually ended up expanding their contract by 20% because I gave them back a lot of their time. That experience became the blueprint of how I cut our department's churn in half. I'm here because I don't just manage accounts. I make sure that your product becomes an indispensable part of your client success. Now, you can again follow up with a short question. I'm curious, when you look at your current enterprise accounts that have churned recently, what have you found to be the main reason for it? You can write down your own version of this three-step formula for your individual situation, and then practice it. Give that speech to friends, family, and other people, and come prepared to that next interview to truly stand out. When you use this formula, you're not only answering a question and telling a great story, building trust and empathy, and keeping the interview engaged, but you're also showing the interviewer that you have a clear sense of purpose, the grit to handle a crisis, and a proven system for delivering results. In this job market in 2026, everyone has the right keywords on their resume, everyone has the degrees and the qualifications. But very few people can tell a story that can make the interviewer feel like they already know what it's like working with you. Stop being a list with names and titles, and start being the hero who solves problems. Use this approach and walk into your next interview knowing that the first 120 seconds of tell me about yourself belong to you. Now, let me know what you think about it in the comments, subscribe for more content like this, and thanks for watching.

title: Final Round Interview with Senior Level Executives (Tips and Strategies)
description:
C-Suite executives operate differently. To survive a final round interview with them, here’s what you need to know. 

Landing a seat across from a C-suite executive is the final hurdle, but many high-performers fail here because they treat it like a standard technical interview. 

In this video, I’m pulling back the curtain on the 5 critical hacks I used to win over CEOs and land roles in the high-stakes worlds of banking and consulting.

We move beyond your CV and dive into the psychology of leadership. Whether you are facing a visionary extrovert who loves the sound of their own voice or a data-driven introvert who values logic above all else, you need a specific strategy. 

We discuss how to stop "fan-girling" over the CEO and how to start engaging them in a way that proves you are a high-autonomy, low-risk hire.

What you’ll learn in this video:
* The "Extrovert vs. Introvert" Strategy: How to read the room and adapt your communication style to match theirs.
* The 80/20 Rule of Time: Why focusing on the future (not the past) is the only way to speak an executive's language.
* Critical Thinking: How to respectfully challenge a CEO’s vision to stand out as a top-tier hire.
* Avoiding the "Task Trap": Why you must stop talking about day-to-day tasks and start talking about bottom-line impact.
* The "Self-Correcting" Leader: How to frame yourself as a low-maintenance, high-value asset.

Timestamps:
00:00 - Intro
00:17 - #1: Know your Audience 
03:28 - #2: Focus on the Future 
04:25 - #3 Think Critically
05:32 - #4: Be Time-Sensitive 
06:21 - #5: Show your Low-Risk
07:02 - Final Thoughts 

Work With Me:
Ready to nail your upcoming interview? Book a Free Discovery Call to discuss your interview approach and how we can refine your strategy:  https://calendly.com/larahadry521/30min

#CareerAdvice #ExecutiveInterview #InterviewTips #JobSearch #Banking #Consulting #CSuite #CareerGrowth #LeadershipSkills #InterviewHacks
transcript: You've survived three rounds of interviews and you've proven you can do the job, but now you're facing the C-suite executives and they don't care about your day-to-day tasks. They're looking for chemistry, compatibility, and that wow factor. I'll share with you the five critical hacks I used to win over CEOs in the banking and consulting industry. The first and most important one, know your audience. When you're about to meet the CEO, remember that you very likely passed the professional and the technical screening already. Now, it's highly likely that you're being matched against other candidates that have met the same criteria. That makes it all the more important that you come across as likable and memorable to stand out from other applicants. For that, you first need to know who's sitting in front of you. As we know, many executives don't climb the corporate ladder because of their technical skills, but more so because of their communication and their social skills. That means a lot of the time your exec interviews will be with people that like to talk and that like to talk about themselves. For this type of person, make sure you don't interrupt them when they're speaking and give them as much time and space to talk about themselves and talk about the company as possible. This will make them feel good about themselves when they're leaving the room and will leave a positive association with you. When I was interviewing for a role at the bank in one of the last phases of the interview process, I had to meet one member of the board. I was rather junior at the time and I remember clearly getting ready to impress the member of the board with all of my achievements that I had done in my career. Eventually though, during the call, I could sense that he was way more interested in talking about himself and me asking him questions. So, to please the extrovert type, even if they are asking a question to you, after you've answered it, you can throw back a question at them. This way, it will seem more like a conversation and less like an interview. For example, when they ask you, "Why do you want to work here?" After you've given your answer, you can ask the following question, "What made you choose to join this company specifically?" This will get them to talk about themselves. When they ask, "Are there any changes that you would like to see in our organization?" After giving your answer, you can say, "What are the biggest challenges this organization is facing within the next 5 years from your point of view?" Also, make sure to research them beforehand thoroughly. Check their LinkedIn and look for any kind of similarity that you can find. For example, maybe they speak a foreign language that you speak as well. Maybe they did a semester abroad in the same city as you did. Maybe they posted about their dog and you're a dog parent as well. Bring it up in conversation to create that mutual likability and to create that and that spark. Now, sometimes though, you will find the kind of person that is more of an introvert in executive positions and who might have actually gotten the job because of their technical skills. From my experience, this is less often the case, but you still need to be prepared for that case. Unlike the extroverts, they will not fill the silence for you. They will much rather sit back and evaluate how you structure your thoughts. Here, if you give short, one-sentence answers, the energy in the room will die. Your focus should be on giving a structured answer while keeping the other person engaged. For example, if they ask you how you handled a difficult project, you can say, "I approached that challenge through three specific lenses: the data, the timeline, and the people." Then walk them through all of these points. It shows that you can structure your thoughts and makes it easier for the other person to actually follow you along. This structured response is both applicable to extroverts and introverts. Of course, this categorization into extroverts and introverts is quite a black and white thinking and the reality is way more complex than that. You can use these techniques as a guide post when you're going into your next executive interview. Hack number two, focus on the future. Executives live in the future. 10% of their job is looking at what we're doing today and the other 90% is steering the company towards what happens and what matters in the next two to five years. If you spent the whole interview looking in the rearview mirror of your CV, you're not really speaking their language. The hack here is the 80/20 rule. If you're being asked about a past project or a task that you've been doing, spend 20% of your time on what happened and 80% on what lessons you learned and more importantly, how you going to apply your knowledge to this position that you're applying for. Don't just say, "I managed that project." You can say, "Managing that project taught me how to align conflicting stakeholders under pressure." The skill I plan to use here to help you navigate the current transition into AI-driven workflows. This way you're showing them that you're not just chronologically repeating your own career. You have a growth mindset. You're learning from past experience and you're already solving the company's problems. Hack number three, show that you can think critically. As much as people like compliments and you should if you can sprinkle in some here and there, but fan-girling too hard can definitely backfire. If you agree with every single thing that the CEO says, they will think of you as a yes man or yes woman and not as a top-tier hire. They appreciate candidates who are critical thinkers. Before the interview, find a podcast, a keynote, an article or a LinkedIn post that they have published where they have shared their opinion or a point of view on a certain subject. And then, don't just memorize it, but analyze it. Talk about the topic with your friends, colleagues or family and develop your own standpoint. When you're in the room, bring it up. For example, I saw your recent post about the shift toward integrating AI into everyday workflows. It's a compelling vision, but it actually made me think about the potential friction in maintaining team culture and human connection. How are you planning to mitigate that as the tech takes over more of the day-to-day? This is a massive wow factor. It shows that you follow their content, that you can think critically and that you are able to engage in a strategic conversation about a certain subject matter. Hack number four, be sensitive to their time. The biggest mistake I see high performers do is focusing too much on the day-to-day nitty-gritty of their job. They start explaining the technical setup of a project, the software they used or the project schedule. But here's the truth, Senior executives don't care about your tasks. They care about your impact. If you're talking in detail about your day-to-day activities, you will bore the executives fast. They will not remember what you have said, and they will think of you more as a worker rather than a leader. Every answer you give should link back to how you can help them reach their goals faster and better. Instead of saying, "I organized 15 weekly sprints to launch the product." You can say, "I streamlined our execution so that the product hit the market 3 months early, which allowed the CEO to hit the annual revenue target ahead of schedule." Hack number five, show that you are a low-risk hire. The final thing an executive is looking for in a candidate, even if they are not your direct manager, is autonomy. They want to know that if they hire you, they're actually bringing in a self-managing leader who will not create more, but less work for the whole leadership team. So, the hack here is to reframe yourself as high autonomy, low maintenance. Focus on your ability to handle complexity without needing constant escalation. You can frame it like this, "I've built my career on being a self-governing leader. I'm looking for an environment where I can take full ownership of my project and team." As I'm someone who delivers the best results when given autonomy and upfront trust, while staying aligned with the company's business goals. To sum it up, know your audience. Identify if they are an extrovert, give them space to talk and connect personally, or an introvert, then you lead the conversation with a structured logic. Hack number two, focus on the future. Use the 80/20 rule to spend the majority of your time discussing how your past lessons will solve their future challenges. Hack number three, think critically. Move from fan girl to a strategic peer by researching their public work and offering a respectful, unique perspective on it. Hack number four, stay out of the weeds. Focus on high-level impact and bottom-line results rather than getting bogged down in day-to-day tasks. Hack number five, prove you're low risk. Demonstrate professional self-sufficiency by showing you can take full ownership and drive results with total autonomy and alignment. I hope this was helpful. Hit the like button and subscribe if you liked it and you want to watch more content like this. Good luck for your interview. Thank you for watching and I'll see you in the next video.

 The brutal data from applying to 100+ positions 
 Why mass applying is quietly killing your job search

It was a very solid resume. Now, we all know that the job market at the moment is really tough, and it's not easy to land an interview at all. But guess how many interviews I got by sending out those 100 applications via easy apply. One. One immediate interview invite. One other company said that it looks like it could be a good fit, and they just wanted to make sure that I'm aware that it required relocation. So, that one could have potentially also converted. So, let's give it the benefit of the doubt, and let's say that this would have also counted towards the interview invites. That makes out of 100 applications sent via easy apply via LinkedIn two interview invites, so a 2% interview rate. The other 96 companies had all sent either immediate rejections or rejection emails over the course of several days. That is a 96% rejection rate. This is shocking. I mean, I knew the job market was bad, but that Now, let's move on to the other side of the experiment. Remember, I used the exact same template, work experience, certifications, degrees, language fluency, everything was the same except for the order of the bullets. Easy apply is like the Tinder of job hunting. They don't actually care if this is true or not because obviously you're just applying for jobs so you can get salary so you can actually put food in your mouth, but let's forget about that for now. And what you write in that cover letter or in your application matters big time. I don't just repeat all of my experience that I put in the CV or telling them why I'm such a great candidate. Because you have to keep in mind right now we're seeing an employer's market, where companies hold more power. It's not like back in the days where companies were desperately seeking for skilled workers and would happily take on any kind of person that walked into the office with a degree. Don't get me wrong, companies are still looking for a skilled workers, just a new type of worker. They also call it the new collar workers. These are people that can actually showcase their experience and skills and the actual value that they can add to a company instead of just a listing and boasting about their certifications and credentials that they gathered over the years. And I screenshotted them, made kind of like an avatar for each person, put it on a slide, and that was already a lot of credibility added to what I said in the cover letter my strengths were. Now, this way you've not only increased your chances of getting invited to an interview drastically because you're standing out from other applicants, but you also prepared halfway for the interview already, which will make you feel more confident and more relaxed once you actually get invited to the interview. You might think that this is less efficient and you're wasting time, but in reality, there's a difference between being efficient and being effective. Yes, you're efficient sending out over 100 applications via easy apply within a week, but it's not effective if you end up getting 96 rejections. Effectiveness is more important than efficiency. You can take back a bit of control of finding a job in this employees job market by applying with intent and purposefully stand out from other applicants. title: The exact moment I knew Ididn‘t get the job (before they even called)
description:
Most people leave an interview thinking it went fine. I did too. But looking back, every sign was already there — I just didn't know what I was reading.

In this video, I'm sharing the exact moments that told me I wouldn't get the job — before the rejection call ever came. These aren't obvious interview mistakes. They're subtle, easy to miss, and most candidates walk right past them.

What I'll cover in this video:

Why "we're not rushing to fill this position" is a red flag

transcript: I've recently been laid off and had several interviews for open positions. transcript: I used to think that landing a job was the perfect science where if I just check every box and have this very polished resume, I would eventually get the job. You also need to like the energy of the hiring manager because if you feel completely drained, uncomfortable, or anxious after your conversation, you might want to trust that gut feeling and rethink if you want to work with that person on a daily basis. But you working in a toxic work environment will make you sick in the long term and that's kind of a short-sighted decision to be made that is simply rooted in fear. Now a little anecdote here, back when I was doing my bachelor's degree I was applying for a working student position in a company outside of the city and I had to take three different buses to get there and walk eventually the last 15 minutes along an expressway and I remember thinking to myself, okay, if I am to do this two to three times per week, I really have to like these people. And I also didn't ask because I was not mad about it. I would have not wanted to work there. And for my personal experience, after a couple of weeks, I landed a job at a different company where some of my friends were working at, as well. And I was definitely feeling way more comfortable in that team, and I just like the people. Tech number two, connection can be intentional without it being fake. Now, even though there are natural ways that people's energies click or don't click, there are also some strategies that you can put into place to give this kind of connection a little bit more of a push. I know some of you you're thinking of small talk as being fake. But, it doesn't need to be fake. It can be actual intentional connecting. And how you can do this is by researching a person before you step into a room with them. Check their LinkedIn, and don't check necessarily only their professional background, but check what they last posted, maybe about their vacation, check about any interests or hobbies they mentioned, check if they have any voluntary organizations they like to do work with, or if they are maybe from the same small town as you, maybe they have come from a different country and you can even connect on how it is being a foreigner to a new country. Just things like that that you can genuinely connect on, which will make you like them more and them like you more, too. So, this can be a little bit of a strategy to have a specific pre-planned topic that you have ready, so you don't feel so much pressure of having to perform small talk in the moment. And if you find it hard to remember these details, just write them down on a list and have the notes with you and take a look at your notes during the interview, so you remember what you actually wanted to connect over. Tech number three, people need to remember you to hire you. Now, finally, after we've talked about that people like to hire people that they like, it needs to be a mutual fit, and you can put some strategies into place to find true connection with people. You need to do one last thing, and that is to be memorable. Because of how subjective all of this is, you kind of want to give them a hook that they can take with them when they leave the room. For this, you need a human fact, something that is not in your CV, something about your personality, positive trait like persistence, weird sense of humor, or curiosity. Try not to be afraid that sharing a personal quirk will make you look less professional. Actually, it will just make you look more real and more memorable. For example, in an interview, I had shared that I recently learned how to scuba dive, even though I was really hesitant to try it out because I was really scared of how this whole breathing underwater functions, and it showcased how I was able to step out of my comfort zone and face fear head-on, which was also relevant to this role and to many other roles, and in particular because I had to talk to board-level members. And in that sense, they're kind of like the sharks of the dry land, and I sealed it all with showing a 10-second video of coming really close to a manta ray, and that's done. I was being memorable and eventually got the job. Look, interviewing is tough, and I'm still learning every day, but by focusing on some of these human elements like mutual likability, intentional connecting, and staying memorable, you can kind of take some of that control back. If you're really struggling with that, you can book a call with me and get some tips on how to make this work for you personally, and I'll put the link in the description. I'd love to know which of these points you struggle with most or what your worst interview story is. So, drop a comment below and let's all feel a little less alone in the process. Thanks for watching.

 What the numbers from my experiment actually expose about the hiring system

transcript: So, I made a little experiment. I've been recently laid off and since then analyzing the job market and different application strategies, and I talked to a lot of different people that are currently applying, and it seemed like a lot of us are using the easy apply button on LinkedIn and indeed and other platforms. Obviously, to save time and turn out as many applications as possible, 50, 100, 200 applications per week. I spent the last month applying for jobs to see if this approach actually has a higher hit rate when you compare it to tailoring your CV. And the results weren't only different, they honestly shocked me. So, here's what I found. I applied with the same CV for 100 positions using the LinkedIn easy apply button, and I made sure that the experience listed in that CV was suitable for the positions that I applied for. And then I went and took 10 of those exact same jobs and applied with the same CV, but this time I tailored it. So, I changed the order of the bullets to reflect the most relevant bullet points for each position. I included a cover letter where it was asked for. I also indicated other information where required. So, for example, my earliest possible start date or salary expectations. And most importantly, I did not apply through LinkedIn or through the easy apply button, but for those 10 positions where I tailored it, I applied through the company's website. And yes, it only took me about 1 minute for each of those easy apply applications, whereas it took me around 45 to 60 minutes for each of the other 10 applications that I actually tailored. Now, I already expected something like this, but the results of this experiment honestly were so shocking. Within a month, I received 96 rejections from the applications that went through the easy apply button. 96 rejections. That is a 96% rejection rate. One of them replied that they found my CV suitable, and they just wanted to check in to see whether I understood that this position required me to relocate, and they wanted to make sure I understood this before they would actually invite me to an interview. Two companies replied that they need me to fill out further information in order to process my application. So, things like my earliest possible start date or salary expectations, which kind of defeats the point of this easy application. And then only one of them actually invited me to an interview based on this easy apply application directly and said that they were looking forward to meeting me. From the other 10 applications that I had sent out through the company's website with a tailored CV, I received a staggering six interview invites. So, basically a 60% success rate. Even though I basically used the same background experience on both CVs. It was just such an eye-opener to what I had suspected already the whole time. Mass applying gets you nowhere. Companies value when candidates put in the time and effort to get to know a company before sending out an application. They will prioritize candidates that apply with intent. And often recruiters even have a filter in their software that says prioritize candidates that have applied via our portal first, which then basically makes it even clearer that you should apply, if possible, through a company's website and not through easy apply on LinkedIn or Indeed. And it makes sense. LinkedIn is like the Tinder of job hunting. You get high volume, low friction, but that often leads to getting a left swipe from the recruiters who get flooded with people who didn't even read the job description. A company assumes that if you're willing to spend more time on their website researching them, tailoring your CV and cover letter, that you are genuinely interested in that company and in that job, and not just in any job. So, my tip for everyone out there applying for jobs at the moment is stop mass applying. Start tailoring your CV, your application, your cover letter. Select a few positions that you are genuinely interested in and that you would actually love to be working for. Research the company, tailor your CV, tailor your cover letter, and spend some time on the application getting to know the company before applying through the company's website. You might think that this is less efficient and you're wasting time, but there is a difference between being efficient and being effective. Yes, it might be efficient if you're sending out 100 applications per week using the easy apply button, but it's not effective if you end up getting 96 rejections. Effectiveness is more important than efficiency, and yes, I'm telling you this as a German. We love efficiency, but effectiveness is more important than efficiency. Now, let me know in the comments what kind of experience you made with mass applying, and thanks for watching.

transcript: So, I've been recently laid off. And since then I've been analyzing the job market, and I've been noticing some really weird things going on. There are so many open positions with hundreds of applicants, but somehow they don't seem to hire anyone. More than one in three jobs advertised online aren't real. So, today let's look at how we can identify these ghost jobs and how we can avoid them so we don't waste our time, hopes, and dreams in applying for jobs that don't even exist. First, let's look at this job, for example. It's been online for 3 months, or it's been even reposted 3 months ago. Over 100 people have clicked apply already, and it's a fully remote position in the United States. It doesn't specify any other location. It is an up to a six-figure salary, and it is for an associate consultant. And now they have a similar position up that's for a senior consultant, also posted 1 month ago with over 100 applicants. Same thing, remote in the United States, and a slightly higher, but also in the six-figure range salary. Now, that makes you wonder, why haven't they filled this position yet? There are so many qualified people who would gladly take this kind of salary, a fully remote job in the United States, and as an associate consultant it's also more of an entry-level role. So, how come they have not filled this position yet? It would be normal to have it filled or at least to move to the interview stage within 2 to 6 weeks. To me, this seems like a the ghost job, which is a job that a company posts even though they're not actively hiring or immediately hiring for that position. And one reason for companies to do this is to build up their talent pipeline. So, they collect lots of resumes so that once they actually need someone and they need to fill this position, they have a whole database of resumes that they can look through to find suitable applicants. They can save a lot of costs because they don't need to give 20 to 30% to a headhunter or to a recruitment agency in order to find a good candidate. So, this might mean that they are not hiring right now. They are just collecting resumes, and if you need a job immediately, maybe because you've been laid off recently, then you will be wasting your time applying for these kinds of jobs. How can we spot this? You can check the date posted. If it's more than 1 month ago and they're still not in the actively reviewing candidates phase, then it is a sign that this might be a ghost job. Instead, I filter for jobs that have been posted first and foremost within the last 24 hours or even within the past week, so to have more recent ones, and then also often I will start my job search with filtering for jobs that have under 10 applicants just to increase my chances of my CV landing on a human desk. Also, you can check whether the job is only posted on job boards like LinkedIn or Indeed, or whether it's actually also listed on the company's website. Because if it isn't, then that is not a good sign and might be another indication. Another hint that this could be a ghost job are very generic descriptions and requirements. Let's look at this one. When we scroll down to about this job section and we look at some of the requirements that they have, keep in mind that this is an almost six-figure salary job, and the minimum requirement is high school diploma with 3 years of cumulative experience. So, that is definitely not a very high entry barrier. Now, when the requirements are set quite low for such a high-paying role, then it's likely that they're just casting a massive net to get as many information across all educational levels as possible. And I'm not saying that this company does, but a lot of companies will use the information and get through your resumes and through your applications in order to sell these data to third parties. Another reason they do this, posting ghost jobs and casting this massive net to get applications from everyone and everywhere is basically to do wage benchmarking. So, if a thousand consultants apply for this job and 90% of them are willing to work for the lowest salary range, then why would they offer the top salary range to anyone? They're getting free market research out of it and it is a way for them to keep their labor costs down. Now, what we should also check is whether the job description has a hiring manager or any person to contact from the hiring team mentioned underneath the job description because if they are immediately trying to find someone, then most often they will have a recruiter who's incentivized to fill this position. While ghost jobs are often managed by the central HR team where there's no one specific person that is accountable to fill that seat. So, if there's no specific person, no hiring team mentioned throughout the whole post, then again, that might be an indication that this is a ghost job. Another reason for companies posting these ghost jobs is the optics. So, on one hand do you have the brand awareness side of it? If thousands of applicants see their logo, go on the website, engage with their content, it will increase their brand awareness. And on the other hand, it's also a good sign for competitors and for potential investors if they see that a company is hiring because it makes them seem like they're continuously growing. Currently, as far as I know, there's unfortunately no law that is prohibiting companies from posting these ghost jobs. So, the best you can do is basically apply these techniques to spot them yourself and don't hit apply. And also what I do is if I get a rejection email from company and they ask me whether they can keep my data, I usually say that I would like them to remove my data and remove my application from the database just because if they rejected me already, it's very unlikely that they will hire me later on, but they might use my data for other purposes. So, in summary, check for the following so you don't waste your time applying for jobs that aren't even real. First up, you should check the repost history. So, be wary of roles that say they were posted 24 hours ago, but actually have been first posted 90 days ago or longer because in a high-supply market, these kinds of roles should be moving to the interview phase or reviewing applicants actively at least within 2 to 6 weeks. Also, you should evaluate the education versus salary gap. So, if you have high-paying roles in the six-figure range with suspiciously low requirements, like you only need a high school diploma, these are often fishing nets. So, they're designed to build a massive internal database to avoid cost. Also, verify the location tags because broad tags, like United States instead of a specific city or remote, often indicate that this is an evergreen post that is more so used for benchmarking across the whole country. Lastly, look for human connection because ghost jobs with no real owner can be kind of a red flag. So, I hope this helps a bit and good luck to everyone out there applying in these crazy times. Subscribe for more content like this and paste a job that you think might be a ghost job into the comments so that we can help each other out. Thanks for watching.

title: Hard Work Is a Lie: The Brutal Truth About Corporate Jobs in 2026
description:
For too long, we’ve been told that grinding harder, staying later, and sacrificing weekends is the path to corporate triumph. But what if that's a lie? What if the brutal truth about today's corporate landscape is that "hard work" is actually a scam designed to keep you spinning your wheels while others climb the ladder? It’s time to challenge this outdated mindset and uncover the real strategies that differentiate the thriving from the treading water.

In this video, we're pulling back the curtain on the corporate myths that hold so many talented professionals back. You’ll discover that simply putting in more hours doesn't guarantee promotions, job security, or even respect. We’ll explore the often-overlooked factors that truly drive career advancement, revealing why some individuals consistently succeed with seemingly less effort, while others burn out trying to prove their worth through sheer grit.

We're diving deep into three critical areas where conventional wisdom falls short. Forget just "working hard"; it’s about mastering a different game entirely. If you're ready to stop the endless hustle and start working smarter—not just harder—to genuinely get ahead, then this video is for you. Learn how to navigate the corporate system with intention, strategic insight, and a clear understanding of what actually moves the needle in 2026.

Don't let outdated advice dictate your career trajectory. Tune in to understand the nuances of modern corporate life and equip yourself with the knowledge to thrive, secure your position, and make a real impact without sacrificing your life to the grind.

If you are working in a 9 to5, working for someone else, no one respects you for that. If hard work really led to success, the donkey would own the farm. Today, let's talk about three reasons why working harder doesn't get you ahead and what actually does. Now, let's get into it. Now, first of all, it's about likability and visibility and not about skill. Basically, the ones who get promoted aren't the ones who work the hardest. It's usually the people who are likable, personable, funny, who tell jokes in the office, and who actually build meaningful relations with their bosses and their colleagues and maybe go for a drink or two after work together. The psychology behind this is simple. People trust and favor other people that they like. And decisions like promotions, they're never 100% objective. People will favor those people and help other people advance in their career that they actually enjoy working with and that they like on a personal level. But that's easier said than done, right? If you're more of an introvert or you're just not really the kind of person to crack a joke, it can be hard at times. But there's a couple of strategies that you can kind of implement to follow that visibility and likability over skill. For example, you can try by giving small but genuine compliments. You can notice little things about someone's presentation or their slides, for example. Or you can make a compliment to them about how a question they raised during a meeting today was actually really helpful. Just small things like this will already start building a connection. Also, try and remember details about their lives. For example, the name of their kids, their hometown, any kind of weekend plans that they mention to you, and then ask them about it. If you're not so good at remembering these kinds of things, just write them down and have a look at it before you have a meeting with that person. It can actually really help. Now, to come across more personable, for example, when you're being asked, "How was your weekend?" Don't just say, "Oh, it was chill. When I worked at the bank in Frankfurt in Germany, I wanted to move to Amsterdam to the headquarters because a I liked the city better and b I kind of knew I had a bigger leverage on my career if I moved to the headquarters. But the thing is that I was only two years into my career so really junior and usually they would only send off more senior or really senior people for these kinds of assignments to the headquarter. But I had managed to establish a good relationship with my boss. We could relate over things like inequality of women in investing. We talked about traveling and working remotely from places in nature. So, we really were able to click on that. And then when I approached her with a couple of solid arguments why they should send me on the assignment, she put in a good word for me with her boss. And a couple months later, I was sent up to the assignment with my rent being paid for a full year, another €1,500 net on top of my normal salary and basically all expenses being paid for in that sense. And when I then told my team about it that I was going to leave and that I was going to be sent on the assignment, I could definitely tell that people who'd been there for longer and who'd been working harder and like longer hours, they kind of thought that this wasn't fair. Now, the ones who don't get fired aren't the ones who grind really hard and are super dependable and reliable, but it's the people that have actually managed to establish really great and meaningful connections. Because think about it, often layoffs happen because shareholders of a company want to make more money, they want to save money, and they want to make their organization more efficient. How do they do that? They do that by making people redundant that can easily be replaced by cheaper workers or AI. And finally, it's about impact, not effort. Hustling for hours doesn't matter if nothing moves because of you. You could be the hardest worker and work the longest hours, but no one will notice if what you're actually doing doesn't drive any results, solve any problems, or bring real value to the business or the client. The key is focus. Try and identify 10 to 20% of the work that actually drives 80% of the results. So, the 8020 rule. And stop doing all of the work around it that doesn't really matter. And also, don't try and do everything yourself. try and delegate and automate wherever you can because your time spent should be where the most impact can be created. The thing was though that no matter how much time I would spend or how hard I would work, the client just didn't seem to be happy. And now I also get why because none of the work that I did brought like very tangible value to them. I kind of worked worked and promised them that in the end there would be value, but there were no in between steps where they could go and be like, "Oh, I can take this piece of information, this piece of value and share it with the board or the shareholders." for example, I cannot say like, oh, after this step, we gained 100 clients or so. Build meaningful relationships, make yourself irreplaceable, and find out what truly moves the needle and do just that. Now, let me know in the comments if you agree with this or not.

title: How to Lie in Your Interview to Get Hired
description:
If you are walking into job interviews and answering every single question with 100% unfiltered honesty, there is a very high chance you are filtering yourself out of the hiring pool before you even get started. It sounds harsh, but the modern interview process isn’t designed for radical truth—it’s a game of signals, and knowing how to play that game is often more important than being the most qualified candidate on paper.

In this video, we are going to deconstruct the interview process and look at it for what it really is: a strategic performance. Too many smart, capable candidates lose out on offers not because they lack skills, but because they fail the "vibe check" of corporate expectations. I’m going to share four strategic "lies"—or let’s call them "professional reframings"—that hiring managers and recruiters actually expect you to use.

We will break down exactly how to handle the most dangerous traps in an interview. You will learn how to answer "Why do you want to work here?" without sounding desperate for a paycheck, and how to navigate the minefield of explaining why you left your last role without bad-mouthing your previous boss. We’ll also cover the "5-year plan" question (hint: they don't want to hear about your beach villa dreams) and how to leverage the "hobbies" section to psychologically bond with your interviewer.
This isn't about being unethical or fake; it is about translating your personal motivations into the corporate language that gets you hired. If you are ready to stop being filtered out and start outsmarting the system to land the career you deserve, this video is your playbook.

Question number one, why do you want to work here? Now, obviously, you're not going to say, "Because I desperately need a job so I can pay my rent and pay for food because we live in a system where I need a job to do all of that." Because let's be honest, nine out of 10 times that's the true reason why. But instead, a clever answer here connects the company's mission and ongoing projects to your own background, your own experience, and then pivots into how you can contribute and help that company get even better at it. For example, I've been following your company's recent AIdriven social media campaigns, and I know you are one of the first companies to experiment with generative AI for personalized short form videos. Instead, always frame your answer around growth and opportunity. You can say something like, I've really enjoyed my current role and learned a lot, but I'm ready for the next step. In this video, you will learn:

- The "Combined Arms" strategy for relationship delegation.
- How to use hard data as "Artillery" to crush vague objections.
- The "What’s In It For Them" pivot for stressed-out departments.

transcript: You've done the work, the team is aligned, and the project roadmap ahead is clear until that one stakeholder steps in. Suddenly, a small change request sets back your entire timeline. Or even worse, you're being ghosted by one of the key stakeholders. You crucially need to make progress in the project. Most project management advice tells you to manage expectations, but they never tell you what to do when one of your stakeholders is a literal brick wall. In this video, I'm breaking down four psychological shifts to handle disengaged or difficult stakeholders so you can stop chasing people and start leading your project to a success. Tip number one, the combined arms strategy. Most project leads treat stakeholder management as a solo sport. You try to be everyone's single point of contact and end up being exhausted while most of your stakeholders are still not really engaged. To fix this, we use a technique that is used in strategic military battles called combined arms. In a real battle, you don't just send in one soldier alone. You coordinate different units so they can protect each other and hit the target from different angles. In project management, that means that you need to start delegating your relationships. And for that, you basically divide your team, your project team into three different roles. Infantry, artillery, and cavalry. For the infantry, you basically want to pair up your project team members with the suitable key stakeholders. So, for example, if you have a more technical stakeholder like a CTO, you're going to pair them up with your lead developer. So, let them grab a coffee, let them kind of build a personal relationship. And when you're in a status meeting, try and delegate the more technical questions from this stakeholder towards your lead developer so they know how to answer it for you. A crucial note here, do not let your ego get in the way. Because as a project leader or project manager, it's very tempting wanting to be the one and only who answers all of the questions so that you feel important within that project. But a real leader knows the goal isn't to be the loudest voice, but for the message to be heard in the room. Then you have the artillery, your data. Now, difficult stakeholders often hide behind vague objections like, "I don't think that this is safe," or, "I don't think we have the budget for this." When this happens, you need to hit them with the hard facts with data, security audits, case studies, and so on. Because when the data is undeniable, the brick wall that they build starts to crumble. And then lastly, you have the cavalry. These are your specialists that you don't really use every day, but only for specific meetings. So you bring in a subject matter expert when you're hitting a wall with a very difficult stakeholder that needs to be convinced. They come in, they share their knowledge, their expertise on the subject matter and then basically convince the stakeholders and ride back out. So for example, when I was leading a high stakes project in banking, I had one technical stakeholder that would rarely come and join our reviews and wasn't really engaged at all in the project. And because I had more of a business background and I was rather new to the company, I was asking one of our developers in the team who had been in this company for a long time and who had been actually working with this particular stakeholder in previous projects. I asked him to schedule one-on-one with him, present the status of the project to him and ask him for feedback. And luckily that stakeholder then actually accepted and delivered valuable input so we could go ahead in building that app. And if you don't really know much yet about your key stakeholders, do your research. Check their LinkedIn, check their professional background, their interests, what languages they speak, and through that assign them to the most suitable project member within your team. Because remember, your job as a project manager is not always to be the smartest person in the room, but it is to ensure that the room reaches a decision and moves forward. Tip number two, the what's in it for them pivots. When a stakeholder in your project is a ghost or is actively blocking you, it's usually because they don't see how your project can help them win. It's nothing personal against you. They don't see your project as a priority. They only see it as another to-do being added to their already heavy workload. Now, sending five more followup or just checking in emails is only a waste of time and will probably only enjoy them more. Instead, you should try and schedule a one-on-one call with them, or even better, when you're in the office, try and catch them at the coffee machine and basically pitch to them how your project can be a gain to them personally or to their department. In one of my projects, I couldn't really get the marketing department to engage in my project, but I really needed them to move forward. So, I called one of my colleagues and I said, "I know that your team is under massive pressure right now, but the reason I'm pushing so hard on this is that our goal is to become the number one rated investment app in the market. And once we hit that, you won't just have another app to promote. You'll have the number one claim in the industry for your next campaign. I want to make sure we all get that win." That is way better than saying, "I know you guys are busy, but I really need those marketing assets by Friday so we don't miss our launch date." Now, quickly before we get to tip number three, if you're tired of only hearing about this in theory and you actually want to practice those high stakes scenarios, I'm building something for you. It's called the project management boot camp and it's a hands-on program where you'll be given real world project cases. You'll have to build road maps, milestones. You'll have to actually lead status meetings with life stakeholders and you'll be given feedback on all of it. So, you can practice these situations and feel more confident in your upcoming PM roles and interviews. My team and I are currently building it out, so head to the link in the description to join the wait list and be the first to know when we launch. Tip number three, provide tangible proof. Stakeholders get nervous, difficult, or disengaged when everything feels a bit abstract. When all they see is gyra tickets and status reports, they'll mentally check out. You see their eyes drifting off, and you see them answering emails during your meeting instead of listening to you. The fix. Treat your stakeholders like customers. Give them something to touch. Try and use wireframes and prototypes as early as possible in the project. In one of the projects I led in consulting, we were building a digital dashboard for private banking clients. And our stakeholders were on board level. So I was kind of nervous to hear what they had to say to our ideas and our visions. But I remember clearly that in one of the first status meetings, they were barely listening. For the next meeting, I had the team come up with a mockup of that dashboard, including their logo and their corporate colors so that it was more tangible what we were building and what they were actually spending their money and time on. In the following meeting, we then showed them a video of a click journey that a typical customer would go through so that the customer experience would become more clear. And in both of these meetings, the stakeholders were virtually raising their hands lots of times to basically raise any concerns, say what they liked about it, and say what they didn't like. And this is what you actually want in a project. You want your stakeholders to be engaged and share their opinion and feedback early on so that you can integrate that feedback and meet their expectations. That brings us to tip number four. Invite everyone to the reviews. Invite every stakeholder to your review or your feedback meetings. Not necessarily because you need detailed feedback from them on every single aspect, but more so to make them feel valued and heard. But of course, because you invite every stakeholder, it doesn't necessarily mean that everyone attends your review meetings. And that can be a trap because later on in the project, they will claim that they've never seen this or they've never been consulted on this and try and jeopardize your whole project. To fix this, you have to make the meeting impossible to ignore. Now, don't just send a calendar invite saying project update, but actually send a targeted agenda a few days ahead of the meeting where you mention the stakeholders that you need by name. So, you can say section two impact on marketing budget review by Linda because people are much more likely to show up if they know that their actual territory is being discussed. Handling stakeholders isn't always about being the nicest person in the room, but it's about being the most strategic. I'll see you in the next

title: Coworkers Are NOT Your Friends (Here’s What I Think)
description:
Ever feel like your office is more like a family than a workplace? You share the same stress, the same "out-of-touch" leadership, and maybe even the same Friday happy hours. But there is a dangerous line between professional proximity and genuine loyalty—and crossing it might be the biggest mistake of your career.

In today’s deep dive, we are pulling back the curtain on the "office family" myth. We’re breaking down the 5 brutal reasons why your coworkers are not your friends and why treating them as such can leave you vulnerable to professional betrayal. Whether it’s a promotion on the line or a sudden round of layoffs, the shift from "bestie" to "competitor" happens faster than you think.

We explore the psychology of the Functional Alliance, the reality of the Professional Vault, and why your personal secrets often become corporate data. This isn't about being the "office outcast" or acting cold; it’s about mastering the art of being friendly to everyone, but intimate with no one.

If you've ever felt the sting of office politics or wondered why a work friendship hit a wall the moment one of you changed jobs, this video is for you. Learn how to protect your boundaries, diversify your social portfolio, and stay objective in a competitive ecosystem.

Watch until the end to learn how to keep your reputation intact when things go south.

Now, let's get back to it. The fifth mistake you can make is rambling without structure. The interviewer asks a simple question and you proceed with a five minute long story with no clear beginning, no clear ending and no actual point where at the end you're not even sure yourself what you just said. This signals poor communication, a lack of structure and a lack of clear thinking. The company I worked for was very disorganized. My team was very difficult to work with." Even if this is true, the interviewer immediately starts to think, are they difficult to work with? And also, if we hire them, are they going to talk badly about us? It creates a trust issue. A better approach will be, I've really enjoyed my current role and learned a lot, but I'm ready for the next step and excited about a new challenge where I can grow my skills. And even if that's partially true, that's not the kind of impression you want to give early on. Let them bring it up first. And if you don't want to waste your time applying for jobs that are way below your salary expectation, you can check for these kinds of salary ranges on websites like Konu or Glass Door so you know beforehand what roughly to expect or wait until later rounds to bring up compensation because timing really matters with this kind of question. The last mistake is leaving a weak final impression. The end of the interview is arguably a critical moment where a lot of candidates have just mentally checked out already. Now, after you have asked all your questions towards the company, which hopefully you have, if you haven't, check out this video where I talk about some examples of questions that you should definitely ask to leave a good impression. And after that, when the hiring manager asks you, "Is there anything else we need to discuss?" And you simply answer, "No, I'm all good. Thanks." You have just failed the energy test. You don't want to end with a flat response like this. You want the interviewers to remember you and you want to show them that you have the same energy and enthusiasm in the 60-minute interview that you had in minute one as you have in minute 60. Think of an interview like a performance. You don't just stop acting and walk off the stage before the lights go down, but you actually need a closing statement to reinforce your value. Instead, you can try a three-step approach. First off, start with the gratitude part. You can say something like, "Thank you so much for the conversation today. I really enjoyed learning more about the team's approach to XY. Then go on with the reiteration. Based on what we discussed, I'm even more confident that my experience in XY would allow me to hit the ground running and then go over to the final hook. I'm very interested in the role. What are the next steps in your process? By doing this, you've moved from the passive candidate to the active partner. You're not just waiting for them to pick you, but you're actively signaling them that you have chosen them. You leave the room with high energy, making it way easier to remember you and to finally say yes to you. So, here's the big takeaway. Most people leave an interview thinking, "Did I answer this question correctly?" Whereas really, you should be asking yourself, "Did I leave a really good impression?" These are just tiny little tweaks that you can easily fix to make you go from almost got the offer to welcome to the team. If you found this helpful, hit the like button, subscribe, and let me know in the comments below what kind of mistakes you've made in interviews already. I'll make sure to reply. And thank you for watching. I'll see you in the next video.

title: Why You Feel Stupid at Work (And How to Fix It)
description:
Does it ever feel like everyone around you is doing better at their job than you are? You make a small mistake, you’re too scared to ask for help because you don’t want to look incompetent, and suddenly you’re trapped in a vicious cycle of anxiety and negative self-talk. If you’ve ever felt "stupid" or out of your depth in a professional setting, you are not alone.

In this video, we tackle the uncomfortable reality of feeling incompetent at work and, more importantly, how to break free from that paralyzing mindset. I’m sharing 5 practical, actionable strategies to help you stop the spiral of insecurity and build real confidence at work. Understanding the psychology behind these workplace dynamics is crucial because true professional competence isn't just about the technical skills you possess—it's about how confidently you present that knowledge to others in high-pressure situations.

We’ll explore why asking questions is actually a sign of intelligence (not weakness) and how you can reframe your mindset to see "missing information" as an opportunity rather than a flaw. Plus, we discuss how to protect your self-worth from subjective feedback and why tracking your "small wins" is the secret weapon for long-term professional growth.

Stop letting imposter syndrome hold you back from navigating the corporate system effectively. Watch to learn how to position yourself as the smart, capable professional you actually are.

Also, many companies in Germany allow for you to be working abroad within the EU for tax reasons for around 30 days per year, which allows you to escape the really cold and horrible winters in Germany. for example, going to Spain or the Canary Islands where a lot of people go. I love to go to Portugal, for example, which also at the same time gives you an amazing opportunity to explore a little bit more of Europe while you're there. A third good reason why I'm actually quite happily employed as a project manager in Germany are the vacation days. So, by law, you are guaranteed a minimum of 20 vacation days per year as a full-time employee, whereas a lot of companies actually allow you for more. So, all of the companies I ever worked for had a minimum of 30 vacation days. And my sister, for example, works in a place where she can buy more vacation days from her salary, which is great if you're planning like a long-distance travel or if you want to go back to your home country to visit your family. As widely known in the States, for example, there is no law that kind of mandates any kind of minimum paid vacation days, but these guaranteed vacation days are actually quite common throughout Europe. So, not just Germany, but also the UK, France, and so on. Now, many people say that yes, it's all good. You can take your vacation days, but basically, you'll have a lot more work before you go, and then when you come back from holidays, you'll have even more to do than before. So, it's not that relaxing. But from my experience, that really highly depends on your self- setting boundaries and you making a structured handover. Before I go on holidays, I usually block a good two hours in my calendar to prepare structured handover where I just insert all of the necessary accesses and links, the project status, the project goals, and the next to-dos for the days or the weeks while I'm gone. And then I basically just have a short meeting with the person assisting me while I'm on holidays and walk them through everything and answer any of their questions. And that's basically it. I think specifically project management because it's so structured and documented is a job or a role that you can really well hand over to someone to fully enjoy your vacations. And I also don't take my work phone with me when I go on vacations. Yeah, very European, but I really like to set my boundaries here so that I can come back really relaxed and be more productive when I return. And lastly, one thing that often actually surprises internationals is how Germany handles overtime. So any kind of overtime that you do in most companies in Germany is usually tracked and compensated. That means your extra hours go into a time account and then later on you can use that time either as vacation days or you can decide to get it paid out even though taxes and everything might reduce it. So a lot of people actually choose to just take it as vacation. When I worked as a project manager in banking in Germany, it was contractually agreed that I could set off my overtime so that on one day when I worked 11 hours, I could then choose to only work 5 hours on a less busy day in a project. Also, in German culture, many companies and colleagues lock off earlier on a Friday. For example, in the past companies that I worked in, it was usual that no one would really work after 3 p.m., which then gives you an extra long and extended weekend. of course, if you were able to finish all of your business before that. In conclusion, as a project manager in Germany, I do enjoy quite a lot of flexibility and freedom of choice when it comes to my working time, my working place, my vacation days, or my overtime. And yes, that most certainly comes with a lower salary than when you compare it to the US, for example. When we look on Indeed, for Germany project management jobs, we get an average salary of around €66,000 before tax per year. And mind you, the taxes you pay in Germany are quite high, up to 45% depending on your marital status and many other factors with taxes progressively increasing the higher your income is. When you compare that to the US, you get an average $96,000 per year before tax, which is roughly $82,000 per year. So around €60,000 more per year in the US with in this bracket only roughly around 24% tax on your salary. And don't get me wrong, don't be fooled. In Germany, you can also work very long hours and hustle hustle, but you have more flexibility to balance it out in other ways. In addition, project management experience in Europe is also highly regarded across other European countries because after all, Germany is still the biggest economy in Europe. So that makes it then easier to move within Europe to another position in project management. Now, if you're looking for a project management certification to undermine your credibility as a PM in the German job market, check out my next video where I talk about five project management certifications that are actually worth

title: How To Build a Resume That Recruiters Will Love
description:
In this video, I talk about the 5 biggest project management resume mistakes and how to fix them. Whether you are transitioning into project management or leveling up your career, these resume tips can help you build a one-page, outcome-focused PM CV.

While this resume format works globally, this is the exact style I used to land my PM roles here in Europe (specifically Germany and the Netherlands).

PM Terminology Overview  https://tinyurl.com/PMTerminology

Also, here is an AI Prompt to transform your current CV content into a Project Management Resume: 
I want you to act as a professional project management resume coach. I will provide you with my current CV or work experience. Your task is to rewrite my CV to make it **optimized for project management roles**, following these rules:

1. For Business Experience, focus on **Action  Context  Delivery  Impact** for each bullet. Every bullet should show what I did, the environment, what I delivered, and the measurable outcome.
2. Use **quantified metrics whenever possible** (budget, team size, users impacted, revenue, efficiency gains, adoption rates, KPIs).  
   - If exact numbers are not available, **suggest placeholders or potential quantification** (e.g., [X users], [€X budget], [X% improvement], [Y features delivered]) so the bullets are measurable and outcome-focused.
3. Integrate **soft skills naturally** into bullets through outcomes and leadership, not as a separate list.
4. Keep it **clear, concise, and scannable**, to a maximum of 1 page that prioritizes the most relevant roles and bullets first. Each bullet should be 1–2 lines. 
5. Include **project management keywords** relevant for AI/ATS and human readers where applicable, such as: roadmap, milestones, backlog, stakeholder management, risk assessment, delivery, Agile, Scrum, transformation.
6. Organize experience **from most recent to oldest**, emphasizing progression from operational to strategic project ownership.

Mistake number three is describing tasks instead of showing outcomes. Now, this is one of the most common mistakes I see on project management resumes is when people basically list all of their responsibilities without showing what actually happens. title: Most Candidates Fail At This Critical Interview Moment

transcript: My goal with this video is to share with you three mistakes I made as a project manager and what you can do to avoid them. So, let's get right into it and stay tuned if you want to know what tunneling has to do with it. Mistake number one, promise the world. One of the core tasks as a project manager is managing different stakeholder expectations. And one mistake you should avoid here is making overly ambitious promises. For example, guaranteeing a rapid product delivery. Now, don't get me wrong. It can be really valuable to show that you're going the extra mile, but as a project manager, you're making promises on behalf of your team without including them, which can really lead to difficulties later on in the project. Instead, aim to set expectations at a realistic level. You can do that, for example, by including the people who are actually doing the work on your team in estimating the time and effort it will take to deliver the end of the project results. In addition, you can include buffers of around 15% in your time estimation for projects and be really transparent about those buffers with your stakeholders. But don't call them buffers. Instead, frame them as options to mitigate risks. Now, if you've realized you've overpromised, it's just best to be as transparent as early as possible towards your stakeholders. Own it. Explain it as an honest misjudgment or an honest mistake. And from there, set more realistic expectations together with your stakeholders and your team. Mistake number two, impress through dominance. Now, what I mean by that is once you get a project briefing from a stakeholder or a client, don't just go and try and blurt out all of the fanciest business ideas, business phrases or frameworks that come to your mind trying to impress the stakeholder with how much you know. Remember, the stakeholder or the project sponsor does not want you to be smarter than them. that would just lower their self-esteem. Instead, you want to make them feel like they're the smartest person in the room and you're just there to listen to their needs and support them along the way. Here, you can use collaborative framing. So, instead of saying, "Here's what I would do," try and phrase it as, "This is my suggestion of how to approach this project. What is your perspective as an expert?" This will signal confidence and not dominance and will invite the stakeholder along as a thinking partner because people are more likely to accept a solution or conclusion that they actually help shape. Mistake three, go into tunneling mode. Often when we are stressed, we are pushed into a state of tunneling which is when we're so focused on one urgent task or immediate problem that we kind of forget the broader goal of what we're actually doing.
