transcript: In this video, we're going to talk about what is agile project management, what are common methodologies like scrum or cananban and when to use agile versus traditional project management. Whether you are a seasoned project manager or you're a beginner, I will give you some insights from my actual work experience uh working as agile project manager in my day job. So let's get into it. What is agile project management? Agile project management is a process in which you plan, get feedback and adapt the plan according to the feedback in order to deliver most possible value. What that means is instead of making one rigid upfront plan, you are making a project plan that can be adapted flexibly along the way according to changing requirements and stakeholder needs. It includes asking the stakeholders what they actually want and then taking their feedback to adapt the project plan accordingly. It is to make sure that you don't end up working on a project for months religiously sticking to the project plan just to then deliver something that no one actually wants. In my opinion, agile project management is a more realistic way of managing most projects in 2025 where we live in a really unpredictable world. So think of it as a road trip. You want to take a road trip through Europe. Beautiful by the way. Can definitely recommend. Now you can plan all of your stops, book all of your accommodation in advance, and make a sightseeing plan for every day. But then suddenly the weather changes where you get stuck in a traffic jam and all of the plans you made are destroyed. Here we have changing requirements that call for you to be flexible and able to adapt your travel plans. Or you wake up and you're just not in the mood for the 3-hour hike you had planned today. Instead, you'd much rather relax. Plus, you heard from your local host about a recommendation to go to a spa that's really close by, which you actually didn't find or hear anything about in your own upfront research. Here we have changing stakeholder needs that you could not really predict beforehand. So therefore, instead of making one big theoretical upfront plan, what might actually give you a better travel experience and probably bring you to places that you wouldn't have stopped at otherwise is to make a pragmatic day-by-day plan based on what you and your travel partner want each day. And that way you can actually enjoy the journey and get more value out of it. So remember, agile project management is a process in which you plan, get feedback and adapt the plan according to stakeholder needs in order to deliver real value. What are common agile methodologies? Now, agile project management is just an umbrella term which includes several different agile methodologies. Three of the most common and popular methodologies include scrum, canban, and lean. Scrum is a way for project teams to work together in sprints and sprints are two to four week intervals in which the team works on a certain set of tasks. Everyone in the scrum team has a role. Now the product owner decides which tasks are most important in order to deliver value to the stakeholders. The project team does the actual work and then the scrum master helps everyone stay on track. After each sprint, they all check what worked, what did not work, and get ready for the next sprint, always improving as they go. Scrum is most often used for complex projects like building an app where you have to work in small steps, learn fast, and improve as you go. Camb on the other hand is a methodology that uses a to-do list and visualizes on a board what has to be done, what is currently being worked on, and what has already been finished. The team moves tasks across the board as they are working on them, so everyone knows what's going on at all times. It helps people stay organized, not take on too much work, and actually finish things faster without getting overwhelmed. Camb is most often used when a team has lots of small tasks all the time. For example, like answering customer support questions and they just want to stay super organized and not overload themselves with work. Lastly, lean is like packing your backpack and only packing the essentials so as to not bring anything you don't need and not make the backpack heavier than it needs to be. It's a methodology that helps teams work faster by finding and removing anything that causes waste, like doing the same thing twice or waiting around. The goal is to get the important stuff done quickly and make sure it's exactly what people want. The lean methodology, for example, is often used in factories for producing cars where you want to be delivering faster, cheaper, and with fewer mistakes. In the real project management world, I rarely know any team that religiously sticks to one methodology only. You can combine these methods. You can mix and match them to fit any individual project needs. When should you use agile versus traditional project management approaches? Agile project management is most useful in complex projects where unpredictable situations are likely to come up and when you want to get feedback and improve as you go to make sure you deliver very customercentric products or services like an app or a game. Therefore, it's best when you don't know all the answers at the start and you want feedback along the way. On the other hand, use traditional project management approaches when the steps are clear, the goal is fixed, and changes are unlikely. For example, like when you're building a house or a bridge. So, in summary, agile project management is a process in which you plan, get feedback, and then adapt the plan according to stakeholder feedback. Agile is an umbrella term including several methodologies with some of the most popular being scrum, canban, and lean. And finally, you can use agile over traditional project management approaches when the project is complex and not all requirements are clear from the start. And please comment below if you want to dive in deeper into any of these topics um so I can make a video for you over the next coming days. Now, I'll see you here next time and thanks for watching.

The job market's tough, but it's not impossible landing the right job. If you found this helpful, hit the like button so more people can see it. And thanks for watching. Good luck out there.

transcript: What if you could get paid $200 to $500 per hour just talking about what you already know? I'm not joking. Expert interviews are one of the best kept side hustle secrets. And today, I'm going to break down exactly how it works, and what my experience with it was. By the end of this video, you'll know exactly how to sign up, how much you can expect to make, and what the entire process from invite to payment looks like. First up, what even are expert interviews? Expert networks are platforms that connect companies with professionals who have real world experience. For example, imagine a company like IKEA is trying to explore new ways of improving their delivery service. Instead of only relying on internal reports and surveys, they might want to talk to actual people who have worked in supply chain or warehouse operations to understand what are the biggest pain points, what tools would help, and what is slowing you down at the moment. If that is your area of expertise, you might just talk about it and get paid for it. Now, how to sign up? Signing up is pretty straightforward. You can go to a platform like GLG and fill out your profile. You'll list your job history, your previous experience, what tools you've worked with, what kind of decisions you've been responsible for. And most of the time, you can also just upload your CV or even connect your LinkedIn and it will prefill all of these information for you. You don't have to be a sea level executive. People on operations, marketing, IT or healthcare, all kinds of roles are eligible depending on what the customer needs. For me, I was contacted by a Guidepoint employee via LinkedIn and asked to join the network. From there, I proactively signed up for other expert networks as well. Unfortunately, at the moment, Guidepoint is not allowing unprompted self-registrations, whereas with platforms like GLG, you can just go there and sign up yourself. I will put the links to some of the expert networks that I know in the description down below, including Newton X, which is specifically looking for experts in B2B industries. Now, let's come to the interesting part. How much can you earn? Rates vary depending on your role and your expertise, but once you sign up, the platform will give you a benchmark of what an average hourly rate with your experience and in your industry looks like. Don't sell yourself short, though. If you know that you're working in a very specialized industry, you have lots of years of experience, or you simply know what your time is worth, then you can definitely set your rate higher than the suggested average. Now, once you signed up and you feel like you're not getting enough consultation requests, you can still set your rate lower. Be aware though that once your hourly rate is set, it's not that easy to change it anymore. For most of the expert networks like GLG, you cannot change the rate in your profile yourself, but rather you have to contact your coordinator or the member success team to negotiate a new rate with them. Approach changes carefully. If you've set your rate too low and you're renegotiating, emphasize the experience that you gained and the continuous demand of expert interviews in your field. Also, you cannot customize your rate for individual projects. Instead, you have one rate for all types of projects, which could range from surveys to one-on-one interviews to discussion panels, focus groups, and so on. Also, the duration of these projects will vary from anywhere between 15 minutes to 1 hour or even longer. Rates are usually quoted in US dollars and from what I've seen, typical hourly rates range from $50 to $500 per hour. To give you an idea, I set my own rate to around $300 per hour based on 5 years working experience in the banking and consulting sector. Now, what does the process look like? Now, after you've signed up and set your hourly rate, you will be contacted via mail with project invites, including a short project description. From there, you can accept or deny the project. If you accept, you first have to fill out a short questionnaire on the topic through which the client can determine whether you're a good fit or not. It also takes some time to fill out the questionnaire. from my experience around 15 to 30 minutes which of course is also time that you put in not getting paid and not knowing whether you will get selected for the interview or not. My advice here is to only put effort into filling out the questionnaire if you feel like you actually have experience in this field and you can talk on the required points. Otherwise, it might be a waste of time. But on the other hand, don't let imposttor syndrome get hold of you. Now, you'll have to indicate your availability and agree to some terms and conditions. You're not allowed to share private or sensitive information on your current employer or previous companies. These platforms take that very seriously, and you always get a reminder before a session. As long as you speak from general experience and keep it professional, you're good. Then you will contact it via mail again telling you whether you got selected for the interview or not. If you get selected, they will propose a date based on your indicated availability and you will be sent a link for a video call via mail. For me, usually projects are interviews that last around 30 minutes with the camera being turned off on both my end and the client end. Interviews will typically be recorded so that they can be transcribed later, which you also have to agree to in the terms and conditions once you accept the project. You will only get paid once the interview actually took place, mostly by the minute. So if the actual length of the interview was 24 minutes, you get paid for 24 minutes and not for 30. For me, a couple of hours after the call has ended, I receive an email from Guidepoint with a link through which I can request payment. This email also includes session details like the date, the duration, or the payment amount. If it's your first session, you will now be prompted to put in your payment details. 3 to 5 days later, the money is usually in my bank account. Now, to give you an idea, I've received around one project invite per week, but I've only been selected to four or five interviews in a span of 3 months. Personally, I think this is one of the most underrated side hustle opportunities out there, especially for working professionals. You don't need to promote anything. You don't need to set up a side business. You simply talk about something that you have actual knowledge about with people who really want to hear it. Extra tip, depending on where you live, the income earned will have certain tax implications. Just make sure to track all of your earnings on a spreadsheet. Keep all of the electronic invoices on a dedicated folder on your laptop and maybe even set aside money for taxes if you've earned specifically much through these expert networks. In Germany, for example, up to $410 per year is taxfree under the self-employed activity. In the US, below $400 per year, you have to file a tax return and pay self-employment tax, which is around 15%. But honestly, it's better to talk to a tax expert for in-depth tax advice. In the description down below, you can also find a spreadsheet that I use to track all of my earnings. If this was helpful for you, give it a like or consider subscribing as I'm a small channel trying to grow to be able to share my experiences with more people out there. Also, if you want a full walkthrough how to set up your profile on GLG or how to optimize your LinkedIn to be contacted by more of these expert networks proactively, just drop a comment below and let me know. Thanks for watching and see you next

transcript: In this video, I will go over the top five project management courses that are actually still worth it in 2025 based on my own experience, experience from other project managers and recruiters, as well as data I have collected and researched. Number five on the list is the Google project management certification. Now, this course is mainly for beginners and entry-level project management positions as it teaches the foundational skills of project management. It has less weight in senior level project management positions and is more so for juniors who want to show that they are familiar with the context and are willing to learn. As for recognition, in the US, it is more and more respected by tech companies and startups. In the UK, there is more and more recognition for this type of course, although even here it is more so for entry- level positions. In Europe, this course only has limited recognition. You actually get hands-on assignments and learn how to structure and plan a project accordingly. As for the cost, it is a rather low time and money investment. You need a Corsera subscription, which after a 7-day free trial will cost you around $50 US per month. And people report that they typically study for this kind of course for around one to four months. My conclusion on the Google project management certification is that it is a great way for people that have no experience in the PM field to gain some basic understanding and get the foot in the door, especially um as it is recognized in the US. For mid to senior level project managers, I would not recommend this kind of course, especially if you want to use it as leverage to get a higher salary or to get a promotion. I think in that case it is too basic and it will be a waste of your time and your money. Number four on the list is the scrum master. Now for scrum masters there are several different certifications that you can get with PSM and CSM being some of the most popular ones out there. Often companies want you to have scrum or agile experience but they don't care so much about whether that's PSM or CSM. If you want me to make a separate video on the best scrum certifications, just drop a comment down below. Scrum master certificates like the PSM, which is one that I've personally done too, are specifically popular in software, tech, and organizations that are just agile focused and are delivering digital products. It is well respected and known in the states and EU and also gaining traction in the UK even though their CSM is still more often mentioned in job postings. The course itself covers team facilitation, iterative planning, scrum ceremonies and so on. It will mainly help you stand out in entry to mid-level positions and it will signal your agile skills as well as your ability to work in cross functional teams. I would say it's more so theory focused though rather than giving you actual hands-on practical experience and guidance. From my experience, scrum certifications will be specifically useful if you're looking to go into a scrum master role. Whereas, if you want to keep it more open to hybrid and traditional project management options, then other certifications will be your go-to. Now, the training for the PSM in particular now costs around $1,000, where the exam comes on top with another $200. It is self-paced and typically requires around one to two weeks to study and pass the exam. It is cost effective if you want to get formal recognition for your scrum skills, but the return on investment is not really that high if you actually want to gain practical knowledge. In conclusion, scrum certifications like the PSM are particularly good for entry to mid-level project managers who already know they want to be in a facilitation scrum master type of role in Europe or the US. If you want to keep it more broad and open, I would not necessarily recommend that type of certification as it is quite niche. Number three on the list is the PMACP. So the agile certified practitioner from the project management institute. Now this certification I got myself recently and if you want to check out the video I made about it, I'll put it somewhere up there. The PMACP is increasingly demanded in tech, software, digital products and so on. It is globally recognized since the project management institute is a well-established player. I would say it is more relevant at the moment in the states and Europe um and here specifically in the private sector versus the UK and specifically also the public sectors are still more heavily relying on the traditional certifications. What it does is that it mainly signals to employers that you have modern agile project delivery skills as it does require prior project management experience of at least two years. It is less applicable for entry-level positions and more so suitable for mid to high senior level project managers who are seeking for example to get a promotion, get a high salary or maybe for formal recognition before they switch the company. It covers several agile methodologies. So not just scrum but also canban lean xp programming and so on. It less so teaches you the very traditional predictive project approaches like the waterfall method but it does teach you some hybrid approaches in terms of practicality especially the exam is actually focused around very scenario and situation based uh questions whereas I would say the course content itself is rather theory based um where you will also have to learn a lot of uh ceremonies and artifacts by heart. The exam itself costs around $500 US whereas the training that is obligatory can range from anywhere from 20 to $500 US um depending on where you take the course from. I studied and passed the exam within 3 weeks while working full-time but I would say typically it takes around one to three months. The return on investment I think is very high especially if you're in agile heavy industries and it can actually improve your application and your salary but if you're in a more traditional industry it won't be as valuable to you. In conclusion I would definitely recommend the PMI ACP for mid to senior level project managers as it covers agile methodologies more broadly than the scrum master. It is less cost and time inensive than Prince 2 or the PMP and therefore I would say is a good middleway. Number two on the list is the Prince 2 practitioner. This one is extremely respected in the UK and also parts of Europe um but more so in the public sector or in regulated and traditional industries like architecture or engineering. It has less weight in the US and is less often mentioned as a requirement in job applications. As for the content, it mainly covers project governance, risk management, budget planning, stakeholder management, and more traditional skills like those as it focuses more on traditional and formal project approaches. It is not as applicable in agile or even hybrid project environments. The training costs around $1,000 and the exam itself on top is another $300. It is widely said to be a little easier than the PMP in terms of study intensity and people usually pass it within 1 to 3 months as you don't need prior project management experience. It is suitable for entry-level positions, but I would say it's even more valuable for mid-level positions who want to add extra credibility to their CV. In conclusion, I would recommend the Prince 2 practitioner, especially for mid-level project managers in the UK and in the public sector. Now, finally, number one on the list is PMP, the project management professionals certification from PMI, the project management institute. Now, the PMP is a very globally recognized and respected project management certification. It is mainly great for the private sector and multinational companies in the states and in Europe and it often shows up in job requirements specifically for senior level project managers. The UK on the other hand is still leaning more so towards the prince too. PMP certainly signals experience and the ability to manage strategic and complex projects. In many companies, it is actually a gatekeeper for getting a promotion or a higher pay as it does require 3 to five years of prior project management experience. It is definitely more so suitable for senior level project managers. It covers both traditional and agile methodologies. But if you compare it with the PMI ACP, of course, the PMP is more focused on traditional predictive project management and project delivery approaches. It includes realistic scenarios, but keep in mind that it's also very number focused and it will require you to do complex calculations and even learn a couple of formulas by heart. As for the cost, the training is priced similarly to the PMI ACP, so somewhere between 50 to $400 depending on where you get the training course from. The exam is actually another $700 US on top of the training costs and it takes around three to six months of preparation from what I've seen and heard from others. The return on investment I would say is first and foremost high for senior project managers. So in conclusion, if you have a lot of time and money to spend, but you are a senior level project manager in the states or in Europe, then you should definitely go for it as it can add a lot of value to your application, to your CV, and to your job on a daily basis. What you can always do is scan job search pages like Indeed or LinkedIn. transcript: Before spending hundreds or thousands on a project management certification like PMP, ACP or Prince 2, a lot of people ask the same question. Is it really worth it? What kind of job can I land with it? And how much salary can I expect to earn? In this video, we'll look at six career opportunities that open up after getting certified. If you find this helpful, please don't forget to subscribe for more career focused project management insights. Now, let's get into it. We'll start with entry level and early career roles which are anywhere between zero to three years of experience. First up, project coordinator. As a project coordinator, you will support in project planning, scheduling, and reporting, as well as tracking budgets and timelines while communicating updates to stakeholders. The average salary can range anywhere from around 40,000 to 70,000 US depending on your experience and the role and industry you're in. You will mainly need skills in structuring and organizing as well as communicating and time management. The pros of this kind of role is that you get an excellent introduction to project management and exposure to working in cross functional teams. The cons to this role are that it's more administrative work and you have less autonomy while your growth largely depends on your mentorship and the organization size. In terms of market demand at the moment, it's rather medium to low because with AI coming into place, a lot of these administrative works will be automated in the near future. Industries higher in demand are typically IT, construction, finance, and tech. If you're in the early stage of your career and you're considering going into project coordinator role, then the certifications that would be suitable here would be the CAPM or the Prince 2 foundation, which are both more introductory courses to project management in general and don't require any prior working experience. Second up is business analyst. Here, a large part of your work will be to gather business requirements and analyze the data to then translate those requirements into technical solutions. You will also be responsible for documentation, validation and testing, but also you will be assisting in project delivery, budgeting, timeline, and so on. On average, the salary can range from $46,000 to $90,000. Again, largely depending on your experience, the role, and the actual industry you're in. The skills you'll need for that kind of role largely involve being able to understand the business requirements and then being able to clearly and simply communicate them. So for the largest part this will require you to think analytically and be able to use tools like Excel, SQL, Gyra, Confluence and so on. Also you should have a basic understanding of agile and scrum as it is demanded in a lot of industries nowadays. The pros to that kind of role is that you get exposed to both the business and the tech side while you build analytical and communicational skills. It's a great entry point into project management but also into consulting and really transferable between different industries. On the contrary, it can be quite documentationheavy and you're typically not involved that much in decision- making yet. The market demand is medium to high because there's a strong need for professionals who can translate business requirements into technical needs. Key industries will be tech, banking, finance, and insurance, but also healthcare and retail. For someone with little to no experience wanting to go into a business analyst role, if you're thinking about getting a certification, I would again recommend the CAPM or the Prince 2 Foundation simply because there are several business analyst certifications out there that require you to have at least 3 years of experience which is not suitable for an entry- level role. CIPM and Pritz 2 foundation on the other hand again they give you great foundation and great basics on project management and will still help you in your business analyst role. Let's move on to mid-level roles which require anywhere from 3 to seven years of experience roughly. The third career opportunity we're going to look at will be the project manager both technical and nontechnical. Main tasks include planning, executing, and delivering projects on time, scope, and budget. In this kind of role, you will need to manage teams, stakeholders, and risks. You will also oversee reporting and project governance, typically using agile, traditional, or hybrid methodologies. The salary range on average with at least three years of experience for technical project management roles can range from 70 to $140,000 US per year where the non-technical roles are typically ranging from around 60 to $130,000 US. In this kind of role again it will be crucial to be a good communicator and stakeholder manager but also you need to be able to prioritize make decisions and handle conflicts for example within your team. The pros of this job are that you have a high visibility as the project lead and you can also have actual business impact while you can slowly start building your leadership and strategic thinking skills. On the contrary, as I've experienced myself, it can cause a lot of stress. You might have to work overtime and you are the one who is responsible for any kind of delay or project overrun. The demand for this kind of role remains very high because globally there's a shortage of especially experienced project managers who can deliver projects on time, on budget, on scope, who can just take on this kind of responsibility and have the experience to follow through on it because simply put any kind of organization has some sort of project running. Here again key industries will be tech, construction and finance. Certifications that I would recommend getting at this point of your career will include ACP, the PMP and also the Prince 2 practitioner. All of these certifications require at least a couple of years of work experience and can actually help you get to the next stage. Personally, I've only recently done the PMI ACP certification. I'll link the video up there. Um, with roughly five years of project management experience, it's definitely helped me to improve my project delivery in terms of soft skills. Um, and whether it will advance your career. Again, it will also depend on the market that you're in and how high certifications are actually valued in that market. Let's get to the fourth role, product managers or product owners. Main tasks here include defining a product roadmap, vision, and strategy while gathering customer feedback to actually be able to prioritize features and tasks within the backlog. In this kind of role, you'll work cross functionally with colleagues from design, marketing, and engineering. The salary on average typically ranges from 80 to 160,000 US depending on your role, industry, and experience. For this kind of role, you need to get good at market analysis and data analysis, but also you need to be good at storytelling because you want to convey your product roadmap and your product vision to key stakeholders. As these kind of roles are typically in cross functional teams, you will need to have at least a basic understanding of agile methodologies. The pros of this kind of role is that you have both strategic and creative thinking combined with high influence and the opportunity to have a direct impact on the business success. On the contrary, in these roles, you typically have high pressure and also you have to manage conflicting priorities from different teams and stakeholders. The market demand for product owners and product managers is really high, especially among digital and product driven companies who are looking for professionals who can own a product vision who can then prioritize features and also measure success to really have an impact. Key industries include tech, software as a service, mobile apps, any kind of digital product, but also definitely banking and finance. I myself worked at a bank before where product owners were the core of each team with all of the products being based around them and with high influence and high strategic impact built on those product owners. Certifications I would recommend here again would be the PMI ACP, the PMI PMP or also the product owner from the scrum organization. Now let's get to the senior level roles. So anywhere with experience from seven years and up. The fifth on our list is the program manager. The main tasks of a program manager include overseeing multiple related projects under one strategic program and aligning those projects with the business goals and return on investment. In this role, you don't only manage one team, but you manage several project leaders from different teams. Salary ranges typically from $120,000 US per year to 180,000 skills needed for that kind of role typically include more advanced soft skills. So you'll need leadership skills. You'll need to be able to manage stakeholders and conflict and communicate effectively. You also should have a basic understanding of change management and transformation. Pros to that kind of role is that you have strategic influence and a broad visibility within the organization. On the other hand, you're managing very complex programs which can put you under a lot of pressure while also it can actually get you involved in a lot of conflicts and a lot of political conflicts within the organization. As for demand in the market for these types of roles, we're more in the medium range here because of course the higher we go up the chain, the fewer positions that will be available. Nevertheless, especially large enterprises definitely need these kinds of program managers to have the program level oversight. As with a lot of the other roles, key industries here will be tech, finance, telecommunications, manufacturing, but also the public sector, having a lot of projects running on large national scales. A certification that would be suitable for that kind of role is the program management professional certification. And last but not least, if you've made it all the way, you can actually become a project director or head of PMO or VP, whatever the name might be. Main tasks here amongst others will include that you define and oversee general project and program management standards across the entire organization. You will need to be able to align project portfolios with the overall business strategy and financial goals. In addition, in such an executive role, you will definitely have leadership responsibility. So you are going to lead and mentor project managers, program managers and PMO staff in general. Salary can range from 160,000 to $250,000 US and above and below obviously depending on experience, the role, the industry, the country you're in. In this kind of role, you need to have executive leadership skills. You need to be able to convince and influence stakeholders across different hierarchies and you need to have an advanced understanding of organizational change management and transformation processes. The baseline will be very strong analytical communication and negotiating skills. What speaks for wanting to get to that part of your career is that you will have really high strategic visibility and influence on executive level across the organization. It is obviously a very attractive salary and it gives you that kind of leadership prestige. On a more fundamental level, you will actually have the opportunity to help shape the culture of an organization. On the contrary, you have very high accountability for meeting business goals and return on investment. You will have a lot of meetings, a lot of executive and board level pressure on you and you will have to deal with complex politics and competing priorities across departments. The demand for these kinds of roles is medium to high. medium because there's few positions, but high in the sense that there's a lot of organizations that are really looking for someone to oversee and someone to take accountability of all the projects and programs running in their organization. Now, this will not come as a surprise. The key industries for that kind of role, just like in the general project management sphere, will include tech and finance, but also government, the public sector, and consulting. certifications that are suitable for that kind of role and that kind of seniority level would be the portfolio management certification or you should maybe look into actually getting an MBA. Now, some general advice at the end. Certifications will definitely be more valuable towards the beginning and the mid of your PM career to add credibility to your CV, but to also actually learn some skills and basic methodologies. towards the more senior roles. You'll definitely be hired for your experience and not for the certifications you have gathered. In general, certifications mostly come into play when you're looking to change jobs, when you're looking to apply for a new PM role somewhere because HR recruiters, they will use these certifications as keywords. And even if you have so much experience in that field, if you don't have that type of keyword in your LinkedIn profile, for example, you will automatically be blocked out of that search. So that might be good to keep in mind. I hope this was helpful and could give you some direction as to what certifications to get and what your career pathway could look like. If you want more personalized advice on your specific situation, you can book a free one-on-one call with me through the link in the description. And I'll see you here

 Prompt Used in This Video (for ChatGPT):
I am applying for the PMI-ACP certification and need help crafting my agile professional experience description. I will provide you with bullet points describing my real work experience in plain language. Your task is to rewrite this content into a polished, professional agile project experience summary that aligns with PMI-ACP 2025 requirements:

 What your output should do:
1. Incorporate agile terminology and routines (e.g. sprints, retrospectives, backlog grooming, Kanban, Scrum ceremonies, etc.)
2. Map my activities and responsibilities clearly across PMI’s 4 domains:
* Mindset 
* Leadership
* Product
* Delivery
3. Highlight specific outcomes and metrics I contributed to (impact, delivery, business value, etc.)
4. Use clear, concise, results-focused language suitable for the PMI-ACP application field: “Detail the specific outcomes you delivered while working on products or projects within agile teams, highlighting your responsibilities and contributions to the team's success.”

 Format your response as a single, professional Agile Experience Summary paragraph (~150–200 words). I’ll now provide my bullet points for you to transform: [...]
transcript: Hi everyone. Are you wondering what exactly you need to include in your PMI ACP application in order not to mess up and avoid any delays or rejections? In this video, I'll walk you through the process and share two major hacks that helped me with my application. Now, let's get into it. If you want to take the PMI ACP exam after checking your eligibility, you need to fill out an application in order to be admitted to the exam itself. So when I first applied, I created an account and went through the whole application just to see what kind of information do they actually require before submitting any of it. In the form, they ask for information on your academic education, agile certifications, agile professional experience, agile professional training. Then you need to review your application, put in exam details, and agree to the terms and conditions. Now, I think a lot of these parts are straightforward and you don't need my help with filling them out. So, what I want to focus on in this video is the agile professional experience as this one can be a dealbreaker to a successful application. If you need help with the agile professional training part, I made a video where I go through how I studied for it and what resources I used in order to fulfill that requirement. You can check out my video. I'll link it somewhere here. Now for the agile professional experience, if you already have some kind of project management or agile project management certification, you can upload it here and it will be counted towards your professional experience. So I for example already did a scrum certification which counted for one whole year of professional experience. If you don't have that, you will have to draw the experience from your actual work. And here's how. When you put in your job description, make sure to use agile specific language and not just generic project language. Instead of just saying you led a project, you could say you led a crossf functional team using scrum, including daily standups, retrospectives, and backlog planning. Make sure you include agile language throughout the whole description and use terms like sprint, backlog grooming, product owner, and so on. Now secondly you should emphasize your role in the team and align it with the four domains from PMI ACP which are mindset, leadership, product and delivery because basically PMI wants to see how you have contributed to an agile project. For example, for mindset describe how you embody agile values in your role like embracing constant change and prioritizing customer needs. For leadership, show how you empowered the team, how you were able to help resolve conflict, how you were able to show emotional intelligence, for example, when one of your team members was not feeling well and you were showing empathy towards them. For product, show how you kept stakeholders engaged and how you prioritized the backlog based on customer centric needs. For delivery, explain how you plan projects iteratively and how you include feedback loops for continuous improvement. Now, of course, don't make up anything you've never actually done. If you've never been part of an agile project or team, don't just make it up. But when you have project experience, it's just a matter of using the right agile language and tying it back to the four domains to increase the likelihood of your PMI ACP application getting accepted. Bonus tip, you can also use CHPT to type in your project experience or copy bullet points straight from your CV into CHBT. Then you can prompt it to adjust the description and include agile language and the four domains used by PMA ACP. I included the prompt that I used in the description. So you can go ahead and check that out. Also, if you would like to see the description that I included in my application for the PMIA ACP exam, just comment below with PMIA ACP and I will send it straight to you. I hope this was helpful in filling out your PMI ACP application. If you have any further questions, just drop a comment or sign up for a one-on-one session with me. Good luck with your application and fingers crossed.
